01

The must know brief

Etched is building complete inference systems whose value depends on delivering useful model output at an attractive cost, power requirement, and response time. Its public product description covers silicon, memory, networking, cooling, software, and rack integration. The technical opportunity is to coordinate these parts around inference; the commercial test is whether the advantage survives customers’ models, traffic, facilities, and operating requirements. Product scope

What has happened. Etched announced its first customer rack shipment to Jane Street in August 2026; the shipment occurred in July. A customer statement supports early operation. Reuters corroborated the delivery and financing announcement. Public evidence reviewed here does not establish long-term fleet reliability or a reproducible, broadly applicable performance advantage. Delivery release Reuters

What changed in our earlier notes. Etched’s July release explicitly claims architecture-agnostic support and names DeepSeek, Qwen, and Mamba. The previous answer was wrong to say public company material did not support that description. Treat it as a vendor compatibility claim: a complete operator, model-version, and precision matrix remains unavailable in the reviewed sources. July release

Technical ideas to explain. Prefill processes a prompt; decode generates successive tokens. Many workloads are constrained by moving model weights or cached attention state. Larger batches improve weight reuse but may worsen response time. Etched’s Low Voltage Inference targets sustained arithmetic within power limits; Cluster Scale Memory targets memory access across its system. Whether those approaches win depends on the workload. The calculations later in this packet make these relationships concrete.

Your commercial lens. Ask for useful throughput at required quality and latency, measured over realistic demand. Include migration, utilization, redundancy, support, and model updates in the economics. A customer can adopt a new platform for a suitable subset of workloads; moving everything is unnecessary.

Your research connection. Etched publicly mentions RL environments for kernel generation. That makes your interest in environments and verifiable improvement relevant. Internal agent research, commercial inference serving, rollout generation, and gradient-based training are different activities. Etched July update

Read the three worked examples, rehearse the two-minute explanation, then answer the practice questions aloud. The full packet distinguishes principle, company claim, independent evidence, analysis, and unknown. Toy calculations are explicitly hypothetical.

02

What customers would buy

Company claim. The current offering is a rack-scale inference platform. A buyer obtains a system for executing trained models, together with the software and support needed to use it. Public materials do not provide a complete commercial SKU catalog, price list, service-level agreement, or contract template. Exact configurations, purchase versus hosted-access options, supported deployments, and support obligations must be established directly. A marketing phrase such as “frontier inference cluster” does not answer those procurement questions.

Etched says it co-designs chips, packages, boards, interconnects, cold plates, software, and manufacturing methods. It names TSMC N4P for its A0 silicon and describes its own factory and test/prototyping facilities. This is vertical integration of engineering and production activities; it does not imply Etched owns a semiconductor foundry or fabricates its own HBM. The reviewed sources do not identify every packaging partner, memory supplier, or component contract. Etched technical disclosure

Public targeting includes frontier AI developers, cloud providers, large models, long contexts, and agents. Jane Street is the named initial customer. Its involvement does not establish a particular trading strategy or latency-sensitive trading use case. The exact models, traffic patterns, and economic results of that deployment are undisclosed in these sources. Customer delivery statement

Compatibility and evidence

The strongest public support for broader architecture coverage is Etched’s July 23 press release. Sequoia separately describes dense transformers, sparse MoEs, and Mamba. Both are interested sources. Mamba is a state-space architecture, so this is a meaningful expansion beyond a literal transformer-only proposition. It still does not establish support for every future operator, model shape, precision, or efficient mapping. Sequoia Mamba paper

Unknown. We did not locate a complete current list of supported operations, exact model checkpoints, weight/activation/KV formats, accumulation precision, context limits, quantization methods, or performance by model. Do not import historical Sohu format claims into the current system. “Can execute,” “produces accurate results,” “is optimized,” and “has production support” are four separate milestones.

03

How one model request becomes tokens

Established principles. The walkthrough describes a conventional autoregressive decoder transformer. It is not an internal schematic of Etched, and recurrent or hybrid architectures can retain different state.

Prompt text
    ↓ tokenizer converts text into token IDs
Embedding vectors → prefill through model layers
    ↓ build per-layer keys and values for the prompt
Next-token scores → choose a token → return it
    ↓
Decode new token using earlier cached state
    ↓ append new state and repeat until stopping

A token is a vocabulary unit, often part of a word. The tokenizer converts text into IDs; an embedding table maps IDs to vectors. Each layer transforms those vectors using learned numbers called weights. A matrix multiplication performs many weighted sums together: it combines features in ways learned during training. Feed-forward networks transform features; attention allows a position to incorporate relevant earlier information. Final scores, or logits, become a distribution over possible next tokens. A selection rule chooses the next token. Original Transformer paper

Three memory categories matter. Weights encode learned transformations and normally remain fixed during a request. Activations are intermediate values produced for the current input. The KV cache is retained attention state: keys and values for tokens already processed, by layer and sequence. It is neither a copy of all model weights nor a cache of finished answers. Caching documentation

During prefill, the prompt tokens are known, so their calculations can run in parallel while a causal mask prevents access to future positions. Prefill produces the state and scores needed to select the first output token. Ordinary decode then processes successive new tokens using cached earlier keys and values. The cache avoids recomputing earlier projections, but attention still reads relevant previous state. The generated sequence remains causally dependent. Caching documentation Speculative decoding can verify several proposed tokens together, so “one token per forward pass” is a useful baseline rather than a universal implementation rule. Speculative decoding paper

Four hardware quantities that must stay distinct

Quantity

Meaning

Question it answers

Compute capacity

Arithmetic operations per second, commonly FLOP/s

How quickly can the machine do the math?

Memory capacity

Bytes that can be stored

Do weights, cache, and working space fit?

Memory bandwidth

Bytes transferred per second

Can enough data reach the arithmetic units?

Access latency

Time to receive requested data

How long does a dependency wait?

Having enough storage does not mean data arrives fast enough. High transfer bandwidth does not eliminate the delay of a small dependent read. A network can likewise have high aggregate bandwidth while congestion or synchronization leaves individual operations waiting. Which resource limits progress depends on the workload and software mapping. GPU performance guide

Prefill often reuses a weight matrix across many prompt positions, producing substantial arithmetic for each byte fetched. A single decode stream reuses it across much less work in each step. Combining decode requests into a batch increases reuse; enough reuse can make arithmetic the limit. Long contexts increase attention-state traffic, while sparse experts can introduce communication and uneven work distribution. The useful statement is that long prefills often stress compute and small-batch decode often stresses memory movement. Neither is a universal rule. Inference tutorial

Concurrency means requests in flight; batch size means the work actually executed together. They need not match. A server may have a queue or split a prompt into chunks. Chunked prefill can interleave new prompts with existing decode streams. Separate prefill and decode resources can allow different optimizations, but moving the KV state between them has a cost. Chunked prefill explanation

Read every stage and its sources

  1. 01 · The exposed module

    This is a photographed H100 SXM module, not a rendering. The black PCB supports the central package and surrounding power-delivery electronics. Its cooling hardware is not installed in this view. Labels identify visible regions, not every individual electrical component. Patrick Kennedy’s firsthand photographs · May 5, 2022

  2. 02 · Look closely at compute and memory

    The large central rectangle is the compute die; smaller package positions flank it. Six positions are visible, but NVIDIA specifies five active HBM stacks for the 80 GB H100 SXM configuration. Do not infer active capacity by counting shiny rectangles. SMs and caches are inside the die and cannot be individually identified in this photograph. NVIDIA Hopper architecture · March 22, 2022

  3. 03 · Package, memory, and compute

    The compute die and adjacent HBM stacks are different components within the package. The die contains SMs and on-chip caches; HBM provides larger external storage. Here they lift apart only to make those relationships visible—not to suggest that HBM sits above the die. NVIDIA Hopper architecture · March 22, 2022

  4. 04 · Where the kernel belongs

    A kernel is a function executed on the GPU. Its threads are grouped into blocks; the GPU schedules those blocks onto SMs. Kernels do not appear in a physical teardown because they are software, not a detachable component. NVIDIA CUDA programming model · accessed October 9, 2026

All labels and sources

Official documentation checked October 9 2026. Historical hardware articles explain concepts, not current product specifications.

Board / accelerator module
The assembly around the package that connects it to the server and carries supporting components. The board, package, and silicon die are different physical levels. NVIDIA packaging example · 2016
GPU package
In this HBM-equipped example, the package brings the GPU die and separate stacked-memory devices together through package-level connections. HBM is beside the compute die, not inside an SM. NVIDIA packaging example · 2016
GPU die
The silicon containing SMs, on-chip caches, memory controllers, and interfaces. This drawing uses one die for clarity; products can differ in their physical organization. NVIDIA Hopper architecture · 2022
HBM · high-bandwidth memory
Stacked DRAM near the compute die provides substantial working storage. Model weights, activations, and KV-cache allocations can occupy device memory; HBM is not the same as an on-chip cache. HBM packaging · Inference memory usage
SM · streaming multiprocessor
A repeated compute unit with execution hardware and local storage. A thread block executes on an SM; an SM can have multiple blocks active. CUDA hardware model
L2 cache
On-chip cache shared across SMs. Reusing cached data can reduce trips to external memory, but a cache does not replace the capacity of HBM. NVIDIA cache architecture
Memory controllers
Hardware that coordinates access to attached memory. Data must reach the execution units; arithmetic capability alone cannot remove a memory bottleneck. NVIDIA memory subsystem
PCIe / NVLink
Links connect components such as CPUs and GPUs. Available connections depend on the product and system topology. Communication has costs; connected memory is not automatically as fast as local memory. CUDA heterogeneous systems
Power and cooling
Power delivery supplies the electronics; cooling removes heat. A data-center GPU need not have its own fan: a passive heatsink can rely on server airflow. Cooling arrangements vary. H100 PCIe product brief · 2022
Warp schedulers
Hardware that selects ready warp instructions for execution. Having enough runnable work helps keep execution units occupied while other work waits. NVIDIA SM and scheduler explanation
CUDA cores
Arithmetic execution units inside an SM. A CUDA core is not equivalent to a full CPU core, nor a permanent home for one software thread. NVIDIA SM organization · Thread execution
Tensor Cores
Specialized execution hardware for supported matrix operations and numerical formats. They are part of the GPU, not whole GPUs; not every kernel uses them. NVIDIA Tensor Core architecture
Registers
Fast on-SM storage for thread working values, usually allocated by the compiler. Capacity is finite, so register use affects how much work can reside on an SM. CUDA on-chip memory
Shared memory
On-chip storage cooperating threads explicitly use to exchange or reuse data. It is not HBM or a general name for memory pooled across GPUs. CUDA shared memory
L1 cache
Cache associated with an SM. On Hopper, L1 and shared memory use a configurable unified resource. Actual data paths and caching behavior vary. NVIDIA L1 / shared-memory design
Model operation
A mathematical task such as matrix multiplication. It describes what to compute, not a particular chip component or a fixed number of kernel launches. cuBLAS linear algebra
Compiler / library implementation
Software translates code or selects an optimized implementation. Libraries such as cuBLAS supply GPU linear-algebra routines, so applications need not write every kernel themselves. cuBLAS documentation
Kernel
A function launched to execute on the GPU. Many threads run its instructions, typically on different assigned data. It can compute, move, or transform values; it is not a physical core. CUDA kernels
Runtime / driver launch
Software APIs and drivers manage GPU execution and submit work. Launch configuration describes how work is organized; it does not create new physical cores. CUDA runtime and driver APIs
Grid
The collection of thread blocks in a kernel launch. A grid can have more blocks than the GPU can execute simultaneously. CUDA execution hierarchy
Thread block
A group of threads that can cooperate through shared memory and synchronization. It is assigned to an SM, not etched as a permanent rectangle in the chip. CUDA thread blocks
Warp
A group of 32 threads in NVIDIA CUDA’s execution model. Threads execute kernel code; different control-flow paths can reduce execution efficiency. CUDA warps and SIMT
Thread
One logical participant executing kernel code, with an identity used to select its work or data. A thread is not a tiny independent physical processor. CUDA threads

No fixed one-to-one mapping. A model operation can require several kernels, and an optimizer can combine operations into a fused kernel. Faster kernels matter when their computation or data movement is limiting the workload. TensorRT optimization · Kernel profiling

04

Three worked examples

These calculations use hypothetical models and hardware. They demonstrate bottlenecks and units; they are not Etched specifications or performance forecasts. Decimal GB means 10⁹ bytes; GiB means 2³⁰ bytes.

Example 1 How much memory do model weights need

Assume exactly 70 billion stored parameters, each using the same number of bits. One byte contains eight bits.

Raw weight bytes = parameter count × bits per parameter ÷ 8

Representation

Calculation

Raw storage

FP16 or BF16

70 billion × 16 ÷ 8

140 GB or 130.39 GiB

INT8

70 billion × 8 ÷ 8

70 GB or 65.19 GiB

Packed 4 bit

70 billion × 4 ÷ 8

35 GB or 32.60 GiB

This is only the weight payload. Scales, zero points in some schemes, tensors retained at higher precision, intermediate values, cache, workspaces, and runtime allocations add memory. Device count also depends on partitioning and replication. The customer implication is that a smaller representation may change how many devices are needed before its arithmetic speed matters. Memory allocation background

Example 2 Why long context and concurrency consume memory

For uniform full-attention layers with equal key and value head dimensions, cache size can be estimated from six quantities: L layers, H KV heads, D values per head, T retained tokens, N sequences, and b bytes per value. K is the total cache in bytes. The factor of two accounts for both keys and values.

K = 2 × L × H × D × T × N × b

Assume 80 layers, 8 KV heads per layer, head dimension 128, FP16 values at 2 bytes each, 32,768 retained tokens per request, and 16 concurrent requests. There is no shared prefix, compression, or eviction. Per retained token, the cache uses 2 × 80 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 327,680 bytes, or 320 KiB across the layers.

Retained tokens per request

Retained tokens include input and generated output. The 160 GiB case equals about 171.80 decimal GB, before weights or other allocations. Doubling context or sequences doubles this simplified allocation. Real systems add padding and allocation overhead; some parallel layouts replicate state.

Use KV heads, not query heads. Multi-head attention gives each query head its own keys and values; multi-query attention shares one KV head; grouped-query attention shares several. Fewer KV heads reduce cache requirements. GQA paper

This formula is not universal. Sliding windows discard older attention state; Mamba retains recurrent state; DeepSeek’s Multi-head Latent Attention stores a compressed representation requiring a different calculation. PagedAttention improves allocation and sharing, but does not by itself eliminate the state needed for each unique retained token. DeepSeek V3 report PagedAttention paper

Example 3 Why twice the FLOPs may produce the same token rate

Assume a hypothetical system with enough capacity for the dense 70B FP16 model, 3 TB/s of usable memory bandwidth, and one decode request. Every step streams all 140 GB of weights. Approximate the weight-matrix work as 140 billion floating-point operations per token, counting a multiplication and addition as two operations. Ignore KV attention, communication, launches, and sampling. Assume ideal compute/memory overlap.

Arithmetic time = operations per token ÷ operations per second

Weight read time = weight bytes ÷ memory bytes per second

Optimistic bound

100 TFLOP/s

200 TFLOP/s

Arithmetic time

1.4 ms per token

0.7 ms per token

Weight read time

46.67 ms per token

46.67 ms per token

Larger of the two times

46.67 ms per token

46.67 ms per token

Throughput ceiling

21.43 tokens/s

21.43 tokens/s

The faster arithmetic waits for the same weight traffic. More bandwidth, fewer bytes, or reuse across a useful batch could improve this bound. Real execution will include costs we omitted. This example is our calculation using roofline reasoning: achievable arithmetic throughput cannot exceed either the compute limit or bandwidth multiplied by operations per byte. Roofline tutorial

In an ideal batch of 32 requests, the same weight read could serve 32 new positions, though arithmetic and cache traffic would increase. That explains why single-user speed and total server throughput can move differently. It does not guarantee a 32-fold gain: scheduling, attention, congestion, and latency requirements constrain the result.

05

Models and software across many chips

Dense models and mixtures of experts

A dense transformer executes essentially the same layer matrices for each token. A sparse mixture of experts routes each token to a subset of feed-forward networks. The model can store many parameters while activating fewer for each token, but routing creates uneven demand and data movement. Activated parameters describe work imperfectly; total parameters still matter for storage. Switch Transformers

DeepSeek V3 illustrates the distinction with 671B total parameters and 37B activated per token. It does not follow that every workload consumes precisely the bandwidth or FLOPs of a dense 37B model: attention, shared components, expert placement, and batch composition also matter. DeepSeek V3 report

Parallelism

What is split

Main consequence

Tensor

Parts of a layer’s matrices across devices

Frequent exchange or reduction of partial results

Pipeline

Groups of layers across stages

Activation transfer and idle time if stages are unbalanced

Expert

Different experts across devices

Token dispatch and return; hot experts create imbalance

Replicated serving

Requests across complete model replicas or shard groups

More total capacity; not proportionally faster single requests

Models span devices to fit weights and cache, or to meet speed requirements. Extra devices also add communication and synchronization. NVIDIA’s parallelism guide defines these decompositions; its example training configurations should not be read as inference requirements. Parallelism guide

Precision changes both resource use and correctness

FP16 and BF16 both use 16 bits but allocate exponent and precision bits differently. Quantization maps values into a smaller representation, usually with scaling. It can reduce storage and traffic and, with compatible hardware, increase arithmetic throughput. Rounding and clipping can also alter outputs. Weights, activations, and KV state can use different formats. Validate the task’s quality rather than assuming a lower-bit model is equivalent. Accuracy considerations

Storage and execution formats differ. Weight-only compression may unpack values into a higher-precision arithmetic format. TensorRT’s documented INT4 support is an example: “four-bit weights” does not mean every operation or accumulator uses four bits. Hardware and operator support determine the actual benefit. Etched’s current full format matrix remains an open diligence item. TensorRT capabilities

These boundaries vary by implementation. Compiler optimizations may fuse operations to avoid intermediate memory traffic; the runtime must still execute the resulting plan reliably. PyTorch compiler TensorRT architecture

FlashAttention is a useful example of software changing the economics: it reorganizes exact attention to reduce movement between HBM and SRAM. It does not eliminate the underlying dense-attention computation. More utilization can come from better software on the same chip. FlashAttention paper

Etched’s software recruiting describes model porting, runtime execution across nodes, state management, collectives, error handling, and profiling. Its profiling role spans host traces, transfers, and device counters. These are evidence of the work required; job descriptions do not prove that every capability is complete. Inference software role Profiling role

06

Etched design choices and their limits

Low Voltage Inference

Company claim. Etched describes unusually low-voltage math blocks, splittable arrays, and coordinated circuit, scheduling, power-delivery, packaging, and cooling work. It claims over 80% of peak FLOPs on sparse trillion-parameter MoEs without thermal throttling. A public workload, precision, and measurement protocol sufficient to reproduce that result was not located. Etched technical disclosure

Principle. Switching transistors charges and discharges capacitance. In the common approximation below, α is switching activity, C is capacitance, V is supply voltage, and f is clock frequency:

Switching power ≈ α × C × V² × f

Holding other terms constant, half the voltage gives one quarter of this component. That arithmetic is not a prediction for the full chip or rack. Leakage, HBM, links, host processors, power-conversion losses, and cooling remain. Lower voltage can also reduce timing margin and achievable frequency. A successful design must make enough useful arithmetic happen despite those constraints. CMOS energy model Intel power management

Analysis. The possible benefit is more sustained computation within a fixed electrical and thermal envelope. The corresponding risks include timing variation, voltage droop, lower clock speed, and difficulty keeping additional arithmetic units supplied. Those are general engineering trade-offs, not reported Etched failures. Validation should show numerical correctness, sustained clock behavior, workload utilization, wall power, and throughput after thermal stabilization.

Be careful with “80% of peak.” The denominator depends on precision, sparsity conventions, counted operations, and frequency. Hardware utilization and useful application work are not identical. Ask whether the figure counts theoretical sparse operations, executed operations, or model operations, and which bottlenecks remain outside the arithmetic arrays.

Cluster Scale Memory

Company claim. Etched describes a hybrid SRAM/HBM subsystem with a shared SRAM pool across its scale-up domain and a proprietary low-latency interconnect. The July release makes the shared SRAM component explicit. Etched July release

Principle. SRAM provides fast access near computation but consumes substantial silicon area per stored bit. HBM provides much larger capacity with high bandwidth, but accessing it has different latency and energy costs. Combining them can place frequently needed data close to execution while retaining capacity for larger models. The difficult part is deciding what resides where, moving it efficiently, and coordinating concurrent users.

Analysis. Logical sharing means resources are exposed or managed together; it does not mean every physical location responds equally quickly. Placement, link hops, contention, access granularity, synchronization, and congestion still matter. Pooling also raises questions about failure isolation. We should not infer hardware cache coherence, a unified address space, or uniform memory access from Etched’s marketing description.

Unknown. Public sources reviewed do not fully specify SRAM/HBM capacities, local and remote bandwidth, latency under contention, topology, consistency semantics, or placement policies. A useful experiment would sweep model size, context, concurrency, and device count while showing where weights and KV state live. A pooling claim becomes commercially valuable when this improves delivered latency or useful capacity under the buyer’s workload.

Specialization and programmability

Specialization can remove machinery that is unnecessary for a targeted workload and allocate more resources to useful computation or movement. The more a design assumes particular operation shapes, dataflows, or communication patterns, the more a new model can challenge that mapping. A programmable compiler can adapt only within the capabilities and performance limits of the hardware.

Sequoia explicitly describes Etched as serving dense, sparse, and state-space models. That makes the current proposition broader than a single fixed attention pattern. Investor description However, Etched’s phrase “arbitrarily large” cannot literally remove finite memory, network, power, or installation limits. Interpret it as a scaling claim that needs concrete configurations. Etched July release

A good diligence question is: “When a new operator appears, can you express it efficiently using existing primitives, implement a new kernel, fall back to a host, or must you change silicon?” Follow with time to enable a new model and its performance relative to established models. Etched’s precise division between fixed functions and programmable execution is not fully public.

07

How to evaluate inference performance

Principles and proposed evaluation framework. The unit that matters is useful work delivered with acceptable quality and response time. A server can increase aggregate output while making every user wait longer.

Metric

Meaning

Qualification to request

Time to first token

Request submission to first returned token

Whether queues and network time are included

Time per output token

Average time per token after the first

Output length and streaming definition

Inter-token latency

Gaps between successive returned tokens

Actual tokens versus buffered output chunks

Tail latency

High percentile such as p95 or p99

Population, duration, failures, and load

Throughput

Completed requests or output tokens per second

Latency and quality constraints; input/output counts

Energy efficiency

Output tokens per joule

Same power boundary and request mix

Cost per million tokens

Period cost divided by useful output, scaled

Utilization, support, migration, and redundancy

A common TPOT definition subtracts TTFT from end-to-end latency and divides by output tokens minus one. It applies when there are at least two output tokens. Averages can hide stalls; examine the distribution too. “Tokens per watt” generally means tokens per second divided by watts, which is tokens per joule. Metric definitions

Comparisons must preserve the workload

Freeze the model checkpoint, tokenizer, quality tolerance, prompt/output distributions, context retention, arrival pattern, cache reuse, sampling, and service targets. Record weight, activation, accumulation, and KV formats. Allow each system to optimize, but disclose quantization, speculative decoding, prefix caching, and other changes and revalidate quality.

Also record the serving version, device count, topology, host processors, networking, power boundary, and complete prefill/decode configuration. Per-chip, per-rack, API-endpoint, and facility numbers answer different questions. Chip thermal-design power is not measured rack consumption. MLCommons measures performance under defined quality and scenario rules and validates power at the full-system AC boundary. MLCommons methodology

Our illustrative comparison. Suppose service A produces 10,000 output tokens/s but 30% of requests miss a customer’s deadline, while B produces 8,000 and nearly all meet it. Neither headline establishes the better service. Count output belonging to successful requests that meet the agreed criteria; the request and token populations need not have the same failure percentage. Include rejected requests rather than silently dropping them.

Batching amortizes weight reads and can raise aggregate throughput. Waiting to fill a batch adds queueing; executing larger batches can lengthen a decode step. Sweep offered load and draw a throughput-versus-latency curve. Choose the operating point that meets the application’s targets. Low utilization also changes economics: a fast dedicated system may be costly if demand cannot keep it occupied.

What Etched needs to substantiate publicly or privately

The most consequential missing evidence is a reproducible set of quality-qualified performance curves across representative models, prompt lengths, batch sizes, and concurrency, with software versions and measured system power. Then come full-system cost, migration effort, availability, failure rates, repair behavior, and time to support new models. These are questions for customer diligence; absence from public materials does not mean Etched cannot supply them privately.

Do not compare a current Etched claim only against an old GPU result. MLCommons’ September 2026 analysis identifies Vera Rubin results as Preview and documents improvements from hardware, precision, and software. The status label matters as much as the score: preview submissions are not evidence of broad customer availability. MLCommons September analysis

Analysis. The competition includes complete GPU systems, specialized hardware, managed services, and customer-developed silicon. Incumbents also optimize memory, interconnects, scheduling, and inference-specific execution. The relevant question is which available system satisfies a particular workload over the customer’s investment horizon.

Added learning guide · Research cutoff: October 9, 2026

The GPUs worth knowing—and what buyers actually compare

Start with H100 and H200, understand A100 as an existing-fleet baseline, then learn Blackwell and AMD Instinct. Add L4 and L40S so you can discuss inference outside giant training clusters. This is an interview-oriented selection of commercially relevant families, not an audited ranking of worldwide installed units. Cloud catalogs establish that a product is offered; they do not reveal global market share, unrestricted capacity, or a customer's sustained production performance.

This newly researched supplement is separate from the unchanged original document. Vendor specification means a manufacturer or system supplier's published number; provider evidence means a cloud provider's offering or availability statement; principle means an established technical relationship; analysis means the interpretation or proposed evaluation here. Sources without a publication date were checked on October 9, 2026.

First: a chip, a module, a server and a rack are different products

GPU can mean the processor or, conversationally, the complete accelerator. A PCIe card includes the processor, its local memory, power circuitry and a connector. SXM is NVIDIA's accelerator-module form factor for compatible baseboards; OAM is the module form used by the AMD Instinct products below. These are not ordinary desktop cards you can plug into any server. The package can contain multiple silicon dies while still being presented as one GPU.

B200 and B300 name GPUs. HGX describes a GPU baseboard/platform integrated into an OEM server; DGX names NVIDIA systems. GB200 combines a Grace CPU with two Blackwell GPUs; GB300 NVL72 is a liquid-cooled system with 72 Blackwell Ultra GPUs and 36 Grace CPUs in one NVLink domain. Its aggregate memory is not the memory attached to one processor. NVIDIA system guide · accessed October 9, 2026; GB300 NVL72 specifications · accessed October 9, 2026.

Principle: scale-up links connect GPUs within a tightly coupled system; scale-out networking connects systems. Memory capacity can be added arithmetically, but useful bandwidth cannot be inferred by treating every remote byte as locally attached. A large model may fit across a rack and still spend significant time communicating. Always ask: “Is that number per GPU, per server, or per rack—and what communication is included?”

The reference numbers: exact variants, not generic family names

Vendor specifications, not measured application results. Memory figures retain manufacturers' advertised GB labels; runtime-visible capacity can differ because of units, reserved memory, ECC and configuration. Bandwidth is peak local-memory bandwidth, not a network rate. Power figures use the source's TDP, board-power or configuration-limit terminology: they are not average draw, wall-plug power or directly interchangeable efficiency scores. NVIDIA's H200 page still labels its specification table preliminary; confirm the purchased configuration with the system supplier. That footnote does not negate the separate cloud-availability evidence below.

What the hardware can calculate—and how GPUs communicate

Three different precision questions: how are weights stored, what numerical inputs does the arithmetic instruction accept, and at what precision are its partial sums accumulated? A four-bit checkpoint can be unpacked into wider values before multiplication; that is not native FP4 arithmetic. Conversely, a low-precision multiply can use a wider accumulator. For example, A100 supports BF16 inputs with FP32 accumulation. These choices affect memory traffic, speed and numerical error differently. “Four-bit model” does not specify all three. NVIDIA Ampere architecture · May 14, 2020.

Selected native matrix paths, not a complete instruction list or a software-support guarantee. The format column describes hardware arithmetic, not every checkpoint a serving library can load. A check for native support still needs the exact encoding, scaling method, operand/accumulator combination, operator shape and kernel. The links column concerns communication between GPUs in the stated system, not HBM bandwidth or an external network connection.

Encoding names matter. FP16 and BF16 both use 16 bits but divide them differently between range and precision. Even “FP8” has multiple encodings: AMD distinguishes CDNA 3's FNUZ variants from CDNA 4's OCP variants. A shared bit width does not prove that two formats, checkpoints or kernels are compatible. AMD precision comparison · checked October 9, 2026.

Customer consequence: native low-precision hardware creates an opportunity, not an automatic speedup. Qualify output quality and the actual kernel path. Likewise, a scale-up link helps only when the deployment uses it effectively; measure collectives and request latency on the complete topology. Ask separately about local memory, intra-system links and scale-out networking.

What each family teaches you

  1. H100: the first baseline to understand
    Study first

    Analysis: learn H100 as a baseline for discussing modern LLM infrastructure. Its fast HBM, Tensor Cores and scale-up links solve different problems. Ask which one limits the application. “H100” alone is incomplete: SXM, PCIe and NVL offerings differ. NVIDIA's current page lists H100 NVL at 94 GB per GPU, versus the 80 GB SXM entry above; a two-GPU NVL pair is not a single 188 GB GPU. NVIDIA · accessed October 9, 2026.

  2. H200: a memory-led comparison
    Capacity versus bandwidth

    Analysis: H100 versus H200 explains why arithmetic is not the whole product. More local memory can accommodate more model state or concurrent KV caches, potentially reducing partitioning. Higher bandwidth can reduce time spent transferring that state. Neither guarantees a speedup if another stage dominates. H200's published peak arithmetic is not a promise that every operation runs faster than on H100. Evaluate the complete workload at equal quality and latency, not just maximum-batch throughput.

  3. A100: installed equipment still has economics
    Existing-fleet baseline

    Analysis: older does not mean useless. A customer may own the servers, have stable software and run a workload that meets its deadline. Does replacing or supplementing that capacity create enough value to cover capital, integration and downtime? An improvement over A100 informs that replacement opportunity, but does not establish leadership against newer hardware. Know whether the baseline is 40 GB or 80 GB, and which interconnect and software version it uses.

  4. B200: the competitive unit becomes the system
    Blackwell

    Analysis: more local memory and bandwidth change feasible model placements and concurrency. The surrounding system determines whether those resources produce useful tokens. Compare network topology, serving stack, power limits and price at the same boundary. An eight-GPU HGX B200 server and a GB200 NVL72 rack are distinct deployment choices. Do not transfer a rack benchmark to a single chip or assume the same economics for a customer who cannot fill the rack.

  5. B300 / GB300: reasoning makes headroom valuable
    Blackwell Ultra

    Analysis: long outputs and many active requests keep KV caches resident and occupy serving capacity. Bigger memory can be valuable without a proportional increase in bandwidth. Higher-power configurations make cooling and power availability part of procurement. “FP4 performance” is relevant only if the model, quantization method and kernels use that format successfully. Count quality-qualified completions, not a theoretical number of low-precision operations.

  6. MI300X: evaluate an alternative stack
    AMD CDNA 3

    Analysis: 192 GB of local memory makes this worth evaluating when capacity limits deployment. Fitting the model is only the start: kernel support, attention implementations, communication libraries and operational tooling determine usable performance. Compare the actual model on a supported ROCm configuration. Avoid both “CUDA makes migration impossible” and “changing the device name is all it takes.”

  7. MI325X: ask what the extra memory avoids
    AMD CDNA 3

    Analysis: additional memory is valuable if it prevents an extra partition, expands profitable concurrency or reduces offloading. If the workload fits comfortably and is compute-limited, unused capacity is not automatically a return on investment. Account for the larger board-power envelope. Reusing a software ecosystem helps, but does not remove the need to validate the specific server and workload.

  8. MI350X / MI355X: different operating envelopes
    AMD CDNA 4

    Vendor specification: both offer 288 GB and 8 TB/s, but MI355X targets higher-power, liquid-cooled infrastructure. AMD documents MXFP8, MXFP6 and MXFP4 support in CDNA 4. Analysis: memory alone cannot rank accelerators: sustained clocks, numerical paths and facilities differ. A format's presence in silicon does not prove that every framework operator uses it efficiently. AMD architecture guide · accessed October 9, 2026.

  9. L4: right-sizing can matter more than peak speed
    Low-power PCIe

    Analysis: consider L4 for a smaller model or mixed inference/video workload that fits its resources and meets the latency target. Its deployment envelope differs from a high-power SXM system. Lower board power is not necessarily lower energy per completed task: a task could take longer or require more cards. Measure useful throughput and total server cost before calling either choice efficient.

  10. L40S: versatility has a topology trade-off
    AI, graphics and media

    Vendor specification: NVIDIA lists no NVLink support for L40S. Analysis: consider it for locally fitting workloads and mixed graphics, media and AI use. It is not interchangeable with HGX when a model requires frequent high-bandwidth cross-GPU exchanges. A server containing eight GPUs is not necessarily an eight-GPU system with the same communication capability. NVIDIA · accessed October 9, 2026.
