Evidence of availability—not proof of popularity

Provider evidence: Google Cloud lists A100, H100, H200, B200, GB200, GB300, L4 and RTX PRO 6000 machine families. AWS dates its B200 offering to May 15, 2025, and L40S G6e to August 15, 2024. These establish procurement options, subject to region, quota and reservation rules—not how many GPUs the industry uses. Google Cloud catalog · checked October 9, 2026; AWS dated instance history.

AWS announced B300 general availability on November 18, 2025 and GB300 UltraServers on December 2, 2025. Azure documents MI300X virtual machines with eight 192 GB accelerators; Oracle announced MI355X general availability on October 14, 2025. This guide has not audited their utilization or capacity for your account. MI325X and MI350X specifications are verified here, but this research does not establish a generally available service for every provider or region. AWS B300; AWS GB300; Azure ND family · checked October 9, 2026; Oracle MI355X.

Newer systems to watch: NVIDIA said on August 26, 2026 that Vera Rubin production shipments had begun that month. AMD's July 23, 2026 announcement describes MI455X-based Helios as in production, while some customer deployments remain forthcoming. These vendor statements do not establish that the systems are the most common GPUs or that every announced fleet is operating. Keep them in the competitive roadmap discussion without replacing customer qualification evidence. NVIDIA earnings transcript; AMD launch release.

How to turn specifications into a useful conversation

Principle—capacity is a fit constraint; bandwidth is a movement constraint. Memory must hold weights, KV cache, temporary workspaces and overhead. Bandwidth limits how quickly required bytes move, but caching, reuse and access patterns determine how many bytes actually move. HBM and GDDR describe memory technologies, not a universal ranking of complete systems. More memory is commercially useful when it changes the feasible workload or operating point.

Principle—peak arithmetic needs qualifiers. FLOPs measure floating-point operations, not tokens. Compare the same precision, dense versus sparse execution, and device count. NVIDIA labels H100's 1,979 TFLOPS BF16 figure “with sparsity”; do not compare it directly with a dense BF16 number. A stored four-bit weight is not proof that every operation executes as native FP4. Conversion, scales, accumulation and unsupported operators can change the path. NVIDIA H100 specification footnote · checked October 9, 2026.

Two meanings of “sparse”—do not confuse them

Sparse MoE means conditional computation. A router selects a subset of experts for each token, reducing how much of the model is active on that token. The selected experts can still contain ordinary dense weight matrices. Routing does not, by itself, impose a pattern of zero values within those matrices. Mixtral of Experts · January 8, 2024.

2:4 structured sparsity means a particular weight pattern. In the supported matrix dimension, at least two entries in each group of four must be zero. NVIDIA's sparse Tensor Core path uses a compressed representation and metadata to skip those zero contributions. This requires a qualifying pattern and implementation; arbitrary zeros or fewer active experts are not enough. Pruning a model to create the pattern can affect quality, and the complete application need not speed up as much as the matrix operation. NVIDIA · July 20, 2021; NVIDIA · July 3, 2023.

Interview connection: Etched's statement about utilization on sparse MoEs does not establish use of NVIDIA-style 2:4 sparsity. Ask which operations are counted, what “peak” means, and whether the comparison uses the same model, numerical path, quality and system boundary. The two kinds of sparsity can coexist, but neither implies the other.

Principle—utilization has multiple meanings. A busy GPU is not necessarily near its arithmetic peak, bandwidth peak, or commercially useful output. Small operations, synchronization and data movement can keep a device occupied without producing the throughput a peak-FLOPs calculation suggests. Prefill, decode and communication can have different limiting resources; the mix changes with shape, batching and context. NVIDIA GPU performance background · checked October 9, 2026.

Analysis—power must be tied to output. A 1,000 W limit does not mean a GPU draws 1,000 W continuously; a 72 W device is not automatically cheaper per answer. Measure energy over representative work, include CPU, memory, networking and cooling at a stated boundary, and divide by useful completed work. Check power delivery and sustained thermals: a device that must be power-capped at the customer's facility operates at a different point.

What customers care about—in decision order

Analysis: establish whether the model runs correctly, fits, and meets the user's response target before optimizing cost. An attractive hardware price cannot rescue unsupported operators, poor output quality or out-of-memory failures. A service-level objective (SLO) can constrain first-token delay, token pacing and the proportion of requests meeting those targets. Use the customer's actual targets instead of inventing a universal threshold.

Measure useful throughput under that SLO, not maximum offline throughput alone. Include the real distribution of prompt/output lengths, bursts, simultaneous users, prefix reuse and tool-call pauses. Inspect high-percentile latency and unsuccessful requests. Batching can improve total throughput while delaying an individual user. MLPerf's separate Server and Offline scenarios illustrate why workload conditions matter, but a standardized result still needs translation into customer traffic. MLCommons methodology · checked October 9, 2026.

Calculate the complete economic boundary: server or reserved cloud instance, host resources, networking, storage, software/support, engineering, energy and achievable utilization. Include migration time and operational burden. Reliability affects failed jobs, retries, spare capacity, maintenance and repair. Obtain an actual commercial quote; an internet GPU price is not a deployable-system price.

Test durability of the choice. Can the stack handle the next model, precision or context requirement? Are drivers, firmware and kernels supported together? Can operations staff diagnose faults and roll back updates? A second supplier can offer capacity diversity and bargaining leverage while adding qualification and support work. Quantify both effects instead of automatically preferring or rejecting specialization.

CUDA versus ROCm: portability is not equal performance

Technical background: CUDA is NVIDIA's programming platform and surrounding ecosystem; ROCm is AMD's software stack. HIP provides a runtime API and kernel language to help port CUDA source to AMD GPUs. AMD's documentation describes tooling and compatibility differences; an existing NVIDIA binary does not become portable without work. High-level framework code may need little change while custom kernels or specialized libraries require substantial attention. AMD HIP porting guide · checked October 9, 2026.

Analysis: separate functional correctness, output quality, single-device performance, multi-device scaling and production operations. Test the actual attention, quantization, MoE routing and collective-communication paths. Pin a supported software configuration and compare tuned implementations on both vendors. A successful port proves it runs; sustained SLO-qualified throughput establishes commercial usefulness. Apply the same distinction to Etched's software compatibility claims.

Three practical comparisons to rehearse

These are analysis-led workload choices, not benchmarks, measured winners or claims about a particular customer's requirements.

1 · A smaller interactive model in an existing enterprise server

Compare a right-sized PCIe option such as L4 or L40S with the available Hopper service. Check model and KV-cache fit, first-token latency, token pacing, concurrent users and host overhead. If a lower-power card meets requirements at lower complete-system cost, unused flagship capacity offers no benefit. If it misses the SLO or needs costly partitioning, the apparently cheaper card may be the expensive choice. Ask whether graphics or video also need the server.

2 · A large, long-context or MoE inference service

Compare tuned H200, Blackwell and AMD Instinct systems at equivalent quality. Does local-memory capacity avoid another partition? Do KV caches constrain concurrency? How much expert or tensor-parallel traffic crosses links? Measure the latency-throughput curve with the same request mix. More aggregate memory can still mean time spent moving data; a faster chip can still wait behind a saturated link. Leave operational headroom for bursts and failures.

3 · Reinforcement-learning rollouts plus learner updates

Separate policy inference generating trajectories from gradient-based learning. Compare rollout throughput, environment/tool execution, reward computation, policy-weight synchronization and learner time. Uneven episodes can leave devices waiting for stragglers. A GPU fleet can be evaluated for both phases; assess a specialized inference accelerator only for stages it actually supports. Faster rollout tokens help if they shorten the useful learning cycle without damaging policy consistency or training quality.

A strong interview answer

“I would learn the GPU families through the constraints they change. H100 is a useful baseline; H200 shows why local memory and bandwidth matter; Blackwell makes system topology and low-precision execution increasingly important. AMD makes software qualification part of a serious alternative-vendor evaluation, while L4 and L40S remind me that not every inference deployment needs the largest accelerator. For Etched, I would ask which complete-system bottleneck it removes, then test whether that advantage survives the customer's quality, latency, utilization and operational requirements.”

The question to remember: Which complete system delivers the most useful work at the required quality and latency, given this customer's software, power, budget and deployment constraints?

09

From silicon to a dependable customer fleet

Design → foundry fabrication → packaging and memory
    → board assembly and test → rack integration
    → power and cooling qualification → installation
    → model validation → sustained operation and repair
    → incident learning and software or hardware revisions

Analysis. Each transition creates a separate execution problem. Good silicon yield does not guarantee good assembled-system yield. Packaging and memory availability can constrain production. Boards must maintain signal and power integrity. Cooling must work under sustained, uneven load. Factory tests must catch defects without becoming a throughput bottleneck. Customer sites need compatible power, liquid cooling where required, networking, floor layout, and maintenance procedures.

A deployment then needs provisioning, telemetry, model enablement, safe updates, spares, and ownership of incidents. Etched’s Fleet Software Lead role explicitly covers partial failures, recovery, upgrades, customer deployments, and operational learning. The posting establishes intended responsibilities, not fleet-level completion metrics. Fleet software role

Supplier risk includes delivery timing, replacement lead times, concentration in critical components, and the support roadmap. A customer needs confidence that today’s advantage will remain useful across future model releases. Capital can fund facilities and inventory; it cannot by itself establish yield, reliability, or product-market fit.

Who might adopt early

Hypotheses to test. Large inference providers with sustained demand may value additional useful tokens within a power allocation. Application providers may value faster interactive reasoning or agent completion. Organizations with relatively stable model portfolios and strong engineering teams may tolerate integration work better than buyers with fragmented requirements. A named financial customer is evidence of interest, but it does not reveal its application.

Migration work may include model conversion, numerical validation, kernel enablement, serving integration, cache and scheduling changes, monitoring, capacity planning, deployment qualification, and incident procedures. A familiar API can simplify application changes while significant backend engineering remains. Qualification should establish exactly which party owns each task.

A proposed customer pilot

1. Define an application outcome and acceptance targets: quality, first-token delay, ongoing token pace, total task time, availability, and permitted errors. Include successful tool use where relevant.

2. Freeze the comparison contract: model, sampling, quality tolerances, formats, serving versions, complete hardware topology, and power boundary. Document permitted optimizations.

3. Replay representative demand: short and long prompts, output lengths, bursts, prefix reuse, multi-turn traffic, low load, target load, and saturation.

4. Report useful capacity: successful requests and tokens satisfying the agreed service targets, alongside queues, p50/p95/p99 latency, errors, cancellations, and rejections.

5. Exercise operations: a sustained soak, model reload, firmware/software upgrade and rollback, and representative device or link failures. Measure recovery and operator effort.

6. Calculate full economics and agree on a production gate: include equipment or lease charges, power, facilities, network, spares, support, migration, and reserved redundancy.

For the cost calculation, P is total period cost and Q is the number of qualifying output tokens. C is the resulting cost per million useful output tokens:

C = P × 1,000,000 ÷ Q

“Qualifying” means output from successful requests meeting the selected quality and service criteria. Include input processing in the cost even when the denominator is output tokens. State depreciation period, financing assumptions, energy price, utilization, and failure/retry treatment. For agents, also measure cost per successfully completed task; extra tokens can represent either valuable reasoning or wasted attempts.

The strongest thesis and objections

Thesis — analysis. Persistent inference demand can justify a purpose-built system. If Etched combines efficient arithmetic with faster access to the right data and dependable software, it can increase useful work under a fixed power budget or reduce the cost of a required service level. A meaningful workload segment can support adoption even without winning every benchmark.

Objections — analysis. Competitors are improving the same bottlenecks. New model structures can erode a favored dataflow. Customer savings may be consumed by migration, idle capacity, redundancy, or operational labor. A narrow benchmark lead can disappear at the customer’s context lengths or latency targets. Hardware production and support must scale together. The investment decision should compare a durable delivered advantage with the next best available alternative, including staying on current infrastructure.

Added interview learning material · Part I · Research cutoff: October 9, 2026

Understand the whole inference system

A useful accelerator must do more than calculate quickly. It must receive enough work and data, exchange intermediate results, stay within electrical and thermal limits, and produce correct answers reliably. This expanded learning guide is separate from your preserved research. It develops the technical foundations of the passage you supplied; it does not turn general principles into verified claims about Etched.

How to read this: “Established principle” identifies general technical concepts; “analysis” identifies their interpretation for a customer or interview. All numerical exercises below are deliberately hypothetical, not product benchmarks. Sources are original papers or official documentation; undated living documentation was accessed October 9, 2026.

Request → tokens Compute Memory Communication Power & cooling Software & reliability

1. Follow a request—and separate the two kinds of waiting

Established principle. A tokenizer represents text as integer token IDs. An embedding lookup turns IDs into vectors, or lists of numbers. Model layers transform those vectors into increasingly useful representations. In a typical decoder-only transformer, attention mixes information across permitted positions, while feed-forward layers transform each position. These components derive from the transformer architecture. Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need (June 12, 2017).

The final layer produces vocabulary scores, called logits; the decoding policy chooses the next token. Selection can be deterministic: greedy decoding selects the highest-scoring token. Random sampling instead draws according to a probability distribution, potentially after adjustments such as temperature. Do not treat “sampling” and all token-selection methods as identical. Hugging Face, Generation strategies (accessed October 9, 2026).

Prefill processes the prompt. Many known prompt positions can be processed together within each layer, even though causal attention prevents a position from using later prompt positions. The layer stack remains sequential. Prefill also creates attention keys and values. The last prompt position supplies scores for the first output token; generating that first token does not require an additional ordinary decode pass over an already-generated token.

Decode then repeatedly processes the newly chosen token and its prior context. Keys describe how earlier positions can be matched by the current query; values provide the information combined using those attention scores. Caching earlier keys and values avoids recomputing them. It does not eliminate attention over the stored history. The cache is model- and request-dependent numerical state, not a database of facts or a copy of the model weights. Hugging Face, How caching works (living documentation; accessed October 9, 2026).

A tiny attention calculation: where Q, K and V come from

Illustrative toy, not a real model: Consider two positions with numerical representations x₁ = [1, 0] and x₂ = [0, 1]. Use one attention head with one-number queries, keys and values. A projection is a learned weighted sum; choose projection weights WQ = [0, 1], WK = [0, ln 3], and WV = [2, 6]. Here ln 3 is the natural logarithm of 3. We deliberately omit positional encoding, other heads, normalization, residual connections and the output projection.

  1. Project. Multiplying each representation by those weights gives q₂ = 1, k₁ = 0, k₂ = ln 3, v₁ = 2 and v₂ = 6. For example, v₂ = 0 × 2 + 1 × 6 = 6. Queries, keys and values are computed from representations; they are not three separate sets of input words.
  2. Match. At position 2, both positions are permitted by the causal mask. Multiply q₂ by each key. The scores are [0, ln 3]. Attention normally divides scores by the square root of the key dimension; that divisor is √1 = 1 in this toy.
  3. Normalize. Softmax exponentiates the scores and divides by their sum: [e⁰, eln 3] ÷ (1 + 3) = [¼, ¾]. These weights describe how to combine values; they are not the probabilities of the next vocabulary token.
  4. Combine. The attention output is ¼ × 2 + ¾ × 6 = 5. This is an intermediate activation, not a selected word. Subsequent model computations eventually produce vocabulary logits. The mechanism follows Attention Is All You Need (June 12, 2017); the numbers are our own teaching example.

Why retain old K/V but not old Q? For position 3, the new query matches cached k₁ and k₂ plus the new k₃, then combines the corresponding values. Old queries would recompute old outputs, which are not needed for this step. With fixed weights and the same causal position rules, adding a later token does not change earlier representations, so their keys and values remain reusable. Hugging Face caching explanation · accessed October 9, 2026.

The ordinary autoregressive dependency is important: the next input token is unknown until the previous output is selected. Parallel hardware can work across layers’ internal calculations, prompt positions, or concurrent requests, but cannot simply generate all unknown future tokens independently. Techniques such as speculative decoding change the execution strategy; they do not make this dependency disappear.

Time to first token (TTFT) includes more than prefill: queuing, routing, preprocessing, network transport, and possibly cache retrieval also contribute. Time per output token (TPOT) commonly averages the generation interval after the first token; individual inter-token gaps can still vary. The 99th-percentile latency describes a slow tail, not the typical request. Goodput counts work satisfying declared service targets, whereas raw throughput can include unacceptably slow responses. NVIDIA AIPerf metrics reference (accessed October 9, 2026).

Mechanism → customer outcome: Faster prefill makes a long-document assistant begin sooner; faster decode makes its answer arrive more smoothly. A customer may value these differently.

Say it in an interview: “I would ask whether users are waiting for the answer to start or waiting for it to finish, then inspect queue time separately from model execution.” Follow-up: “How do the target prompt and output distributions change that answer?”

2. Compute: why peak FLOPs are a ceiling, not a product result

Established principle. A matrix multiplication computes many weighted sums: multiply inputs by learned weights, then add the products. A dense multiplication of an M × K matrix by a K × N matrix needs approximately 2MKN floating-point operations when a multiplication and an addition count separately. Tensor Cores are specialized arithmetic hardware for supported matrix operations and numerical formats; they are not entire models, and not every model operation maps efficiently onto them. Matrix dimensions and data reuse affect utilization. NVIDIA, Matrix Multiplication Background (accessed October 9, 2026).

Arithmetic intensity is useful work per byte moved across a specified memory boundary. A simplified “roofline” says attainable FLOPs/s cannot exceed either compute capacity or bandwidth multiplied by intensity. This assumes enough parallel work to occupy the hardware. Small operations, launches, synchronization, irregular accesses, and communication can leave performance below both ceilings. NVIDIA, GPU Performance Background (accessed October 9, 2026).

Attainable FLOPs/s ≤ min(compute ceiling, memory bandwidth × arithmetic intensity)

Idealized step time ≥ max(arithmetic work ÷ compute rate, bytes moved ÷ bandwidth)

The second expression is an optimistic lower bound when computation and data movement overlap. It is not permission to ignore launch time or communication, and sequential work can make the real time longer than the maximum.

Worked exercise: five times the FLOPs, almost no benefit?

Illustrative assumptions: An 8-billion-parameter dense model, 2 bytes per weight, approximately 2 operations per parameter per generated token, 2 TB/s sustained weight bandwidth, and a 200 TFLOP/s arithmetic ceiling. Assume every weight is read once per decode step and reused perfectly across that step’s batch. Ignore KV reads, activations, networking, launches, and capacity constraints. GB and TB are decimal here.

Derived idealized limits—not measured GPU performance
QuantityOne sequence32 sequences in a batch
Weight bytes per step16 GB16 GB, assuming reuse
Arithmetic per step16 GFLOPs512 GFLOPs
Arithmetic time0.08 ms2.56 ms
Weight-transfer time8 ms8 ms
Optimistic aggregate output ceiling125 tokens/s4,000 tokens/s

At batch one, 16 GB ÷ 2,000 GB/s = 0.008 seconds. Increasing compute to 1,000 TFLOP/s reduces the arithmetic term to 0.016 ms, but leaves the 8 ms transfer floor unchanged. Batching amortizes the weight read across more output tokens; it does not give each user 4,000 tokens/s. Real performance will be lower, and increasing batch size eventually introduces other limits.

“Prefill is compute-bound; decode is memory-bound” is therefore a useful starting approximation, not a law. Large batches increase decode’s weight reuse; long contexts increase attention work and KV traffic; quantization changes bytes and available arithmetic paths. Very short prefills may underfill the accelerator. Dense and mixture-of-experts layers can have different limiting operations within the same request. Dedicated prefill/decode pools can reduce interference, but transferring the KV cache introduces another cost. NVIDIA Dynamo, Disaggregated Serving (accessed October 9, 2026).

Mechanism → customer outcome: Removing the actual bottleneck raises delivered capacity; buying arithmetic that cannot be fed does not. Follow-up: “At our required latency and concurrency, is the limiting resource math, local memory traffic, communication, or scheduling?”

3. Memory: distinguish what is stored from how fast it moves

Weights
Learned parameters retained across requests until the model changes. A model’s parameter count is not its total inference-memory requirement.
Activations
Intermediate numbers produced while processing inputs. Temporary activations and working buffers consume memory even when they are not retained for gradient computation.
KV cache
Attention state retained across generation steps. Its size depends on architecture, stored context, active sequences, and cache precision—not only total parameters.
Capacity, bandwidth, latency
Capacity is how many bytes fit. Bandwidth is bytes transferred per second. Latency is the delay before a dependent access completes. More capacity does not automatically improve either speed measure.

Established principle. Registers and on-chip SRAM support fast, relatively small working sets; HBM is stacked DRAM close to the accelerator package and supplies substantially larger working storage. Different structures have different access rules: CUDA “shared memory” is programmer-managed on-chip storage, not a rack-wide shared address space. FlashAttention illustrates why hierarchy matters: tiling attention to reuse data in SRAM reduces transfers to and from HBM without replacing exact attention with an approximation. Dao et al., FlashAttention (May 27, 2022).

Worked exercise: why fitting the weights is only the beginning

Illustrative weight calculation: 70 billion parameters × 2 bytes = 140 GB, approximately 130.4 GiB. Four-bit storage has an ideal packed payload of 35 GB, approximately 32.6 GiB. Neither includes quantization scales, metadata, padding, KV cache, temporary buffers, or replicated state. One GiB is 2³⁰ bytes; a GB is 10⁹ bytes.

Conventional KV bytes = 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes/value × cached tokens × sequences

Illustrative KV assumptions: 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, and 2 bytes per value. Each cached token requires 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes per sequence. At 8,192 tokens that is 1 GiB per sequence; 64 independent sequences use 64 GiB. At 32,768 tokens, the same 64 sequences use 256 GiB. These figures exclude allocation overhead and assume no sharing or eviction.

This formula describes conventional attention with equal key/value dimensions. Grouped-query attention shares fewer KV heads across more query heads, reducing stored KV state; other designs, sliding windows, compression, and sharding need their own accounting. Do not substitute the number of query heads automatically. Ainslie et al., GQA (May 22, 2023; revised December 23, 2023).

Connect the examples: fitting the cache does not make its reads free

Extended hypothetical 8B example: Return to the 32-sequence batch and its 16 GB weight read. Give this illustrative model the cache geometry just used: 32 layers, 8 KV heads, dimension 128 and 2 bytes per value. Each sequence already has 8,192 cached tokens. Assume enough memory capacity; no prefix sharing, eviction or compression; and one read of every existing cached K/V value per step, with perfect reuse across the query heads sharing it. Assume the cache does not remain on chip between steps. Weights and KV reads share the same 2 TB/s memory interface.

Resident KV = 131,072 bytes/token × 8,192 tokens × 32 sequences = 32 GiB ≈ 34.36 GB.

Counted bytes per step ≈ 16 GB weights + 34.36 GB cached K/V = 50.36 GB.
Transfer-time floor ≈ 50.36 GB ÷ 2,000 GB/s = 25.18 ms.
Aggregate output ceiling ≈ 32 tokens ÷ 0.02518 s = 1,271 tokens/s.

Capacity asks whether those resident bytes fit; traffic asks how often they cross a memory boundary. They are equal for the KV portion here only because of our one-read assumption. The weight and KV transfer times add because they consume the same bandwidth budget—even if their transfers interleave. The earlier 4,000-token/s weight-only ceiling was not wrong; it omitted this traffic. We still omit attention arithmetic, new-cache writes, other activations, networking and scheduling, so this is another optimistic ceiling, not a throughput forecast. Memory-bound reasoning follows NVIDIA’s performance guide · accessed October 9, 2026.

Customer consequence: More capacity can admit the batch without making it meet a latency target. Better bandwidth or less traffic may help its token pace; measuring only memory occupancy cannot settle that question.

Allocation is a separate lever. Reserving a large contiguous buffer for every request can waste space as lengths diverge. PagedAttention maps a sequence’s logical KV blocks to physical blocks allocated as needed, and can share appropriate blocks across requests. Its benefit is less wasted or duplicated storage—not a reduction in every stored number’s size. Sharing requires compatible model state and matching content; a cache is not universally reusable. Kwon et al., PagedAttention (September 12, 2023).

Quantization is another lever. Lower-bit representations reduce payload size and may unlock faster arithmetic, but scale metadata, conversions, unsupported operators, and quality loss can offset the gain. Weight-only quantization does not automatically shrink activations or KV state. “FP8 supported” also does not specify the exact encoding, scaling recipe, accumulation precision, or which operations use it. Validate the target model and output quality, not just successful loading. NVIDIA TensorRT, Quantization Schemes (accessed October 9, 2026).

Architecture contrast—Mamba: In the original attention-free Mamba architecture, recurrent inference updates a finite numerical state using the current input instead of keeping a growing token-by-token KV history. For a fixed architecture, that recurrent state does not grow with context length; it is a compressed representation, not lossless storage of every previous token. The memory and execution requirements therefore differ from full attention. A hybrid containing attention layers can still need KV cache for those layers. This contrast explains why supporting a state-space model is a meaningful compatibility question, not evidence of Etched’s implementation or speed. Gu and Dao, Mamba (December 1, 2023; revised May 31, 2024).

Mechanism → customer outcome: More usable cache can admit more concurrent conversations; faster memory can reduce waiting within each decode step. Follow-up: “After weights and workspaces, how much memory remains for our context distribution, and what quality evidence supports the chosen precision?”

4. Communication: identify exactly what crosses a chip boundary

Established principle. Splitting a model can make it fit and shorten local computation, but it introduces coordination. “More GPUs” is not one scaling strategy. vLLM distinguishes model parallelism from replicated serving and supports combinations chosen for model size and topology. vLLM, Parallelism and Scaling (accessed October 9, 2026).

Four ways to use multiple accelerators
StrategyWhat is dividedWhat commonly movesMain trade-off
Tensor parallelismA layer’s tensors and arithmeticPartial outputs and activation shards; collective operations combine or redistribute themLess local work, but frequent synchronization
Pipeline parallelismSuccessive layer groupsActivations between adjacent stagesCapacity scales; idle pipeline “bubbles” and stage imbalance can hurt utilization
Expert parallelismDifferent MoE expertsRouted token representations and expert outputsRouting traffic and uneven expert demand
Serving replicasDifferent requests across model copiesRequests and responses, rather than per-layer reductions between replicasMore aggregate capacity, but duplicated weights

An all-reduce combines values from participants and returns the result to all; an all-gather distributes everyone’s shards to everyone; a reduce-scatter combines values but leaves different result shards on different participants. These are collective communication patterns, not specific cables. NVIDIA NCCL, Collective Operations (accessed October 9, 2026).

In an MoE layer, a router selects a subset of experts for each token. The network sends the token’s numerical representation—not merely its integer token ID—to the devices holding the selected experts, then combines the outputs. All-to-all dispatch is one implementation pattern. Total parameters drive storage requirements, while selected experts drive part of the arithmetic. Uneven routing can leave some chips waiting for overloaded peers. NVIDIA Megatron Core, token dispatcher (v0.16.1; accessed October 9, 2026).

Important correction to the supplied passage: KV-cache data does not necessarily cross chips on every generated token. A partition may keep the KV state needed for its local layers or attention heads. Explicit KV transfers arise, for example, when prefill and decode run on different workers, a request migrates, or attention state is distributed in a way requiring exchange. Dynamo’s disaggregated request path explicitly transfers KV from prefill to decode. NVIDIA Dynamo architecture (accessed October 9, 2026).

Three concrete transfers—not one generic “GPU communication” cost

Independent illustrative examples, not deployment recommendations. A tensor is a numerical array; vectors and matrices are familiar special cases. Which part of that array moves depends on how the calculation and its state are divided.

  1. Tensor-parallel partial result. Compute y = 2 × 3 + 5 × 7. With the needed inputs and weights already placed, GPU A computes 6 and GPU B computes 35. A sum all-reduce combines the partial outputs and gives both GPUs 41. The communication combines pieces of one calculation; it need not send the entire weight matrix. This tiny example would not justify using two GPUs—it only illustrates the dependency. NVIDIA NCCL collectives · accessed October 9, 2026.
  2. Expert-parallel activation dispatch. Suppose a token’s representation [2, 5] is on GPU A, but the router selects an expert on GPU B. A sends that vector and necessary routing information to B; B applies its resident expert weights and returns the output for combination. The moving object is an activation, not the text token or all the expert weights. Several selected experts can require several destinations. Megatron Core token dispatch · v0.16.1, accessed October 9, 2026.
  3. Prefill-to-decode KV migration. A prefill worker creates a request’s cache; a separate decode worker needs that retained history. Under the earlier cache geometry, one 8,192-token request has 1 GiB of raw KV payload. If the destination has none of it, transferring that full cache moves the 1 GiB plus implementation overhead. That handoff is different from exchanging a layer’s partial result on successive steps; the 1 GiB is a payload calculation, not a measured network transfer. NVIDIA Dynamo request path · accessed October 9, 2026.

Interview test: Before asking for a faster link, name the bytes crossing it, the frequency of the transfer, and the calculation waiting for completion. Then ask whether placement or reuse could avoid the transfer.

Analysis. Treat remote memory as a journey with a path, not free additional HBM. Effective time includes startup latency, serialization of the bytes, contention, routing, and synchronization. Aggregate link bandwidth can hide a weaker path between the communicating devices. A logically pooled address space does not create physically uniform access; placement and reuse remain decisive.

Mechanism → customer outcome: Good partitioning increases capacity without spending the gain waiting on links. Follow-up: “Which collectives or transfers dominate the critical path, and how does performance change when the same model spans more nodes?”

5. Power and cooling: follow energy from a transistor to the rack

Established principle. CMOS logic consumes dynamic power when switching charges and discharges capacitance. A useful approximation is Pdynamic ≈ αCV²f: α is switching activity, C the effective switched capacitance, V supply voltage, and f clock frequency. Leakage and other losses remain. This relationship describes a circuit contribution, not total rack power. MIT 6.375, CMOS Transistors, Gates, and Wires (February 15, 2006).

Worked exercise: voltage savings are not system savings

Illustrative assumptions: Reducing voltage from 0.8 V to 0.6 V with activity, capacitance, and frequency unchanged gives (0.6 ÷ 0.8)² = 0.5625: 43.75% lower switching power in that circuit. If a hypothetical system initially consumes 700 W in that affected contribution and 300 W elsewhere, its new total is 700 × 0.5625 + 300 = 693.75 W: approximately 30.6% lower overall, not 43.75%.

This calculation is not a forecast. The same frequency may be impossible at the lower voltage; activity, leakage, memory power, and cooling overhead may change. Energy per completed task depends on power multiplied by runtime, so a power reduction accompanied by a large slowdown is not automatically an efficiency win.

Lower supply voltage generally reduces timing margin: signals must still settle before the next clock edge despite process variation, temperature changes, and momentary voltage droop. A voltage drop caused by sudden current demand is a power-delivery problem, not necessarily a heat problem. Designers may trade frequency, additional parallel circuits, scheduling, and supply regulation against one another. This is general circuit reasoning—not a disclosure of how any particular accelerator implements low-voltage operation.

Thermal throttling means limiting performance because temperature constraints require it. Power-limit enforcement can also lower clocks without a thermal limit being reached. NVIDIA exposes separate power and thermal clock-event reasons, which helps distinguish them. A short run from a cool start cannot demonstrate sustained behavior. NVIDIA System Management Interface documentation (accessed October 9, 2026).

Analysis. Cooling carries heat away; it does not abolish the electricity used. The relevant boundary may include memory, CPUs, network switches, conversion losses, fans, and pumps. A liquid-cooled rack also needs an appropriate coolant loop, heat rejection, monitoring, and service procedures. Ask about sustained performance at the stated inlet conditions and power cap, not simply whether the package can survive a peak wattage.

Mechanism → customer outcome: Lower energy per useful token can improve power-limited site capacity, but only if timing correctness and sustained throughput survive. Follow-up: “At which measurement boundary, ambient conditions, workload, and duration was the efficiency result obtained?”

6. Software and reliability: make the fast path operable

A kernel is software, not a physical GPU component. It is a function launched for execution on the GPU. In CUDA, a launch organizes parallel threads into blocks and a grid; a streaming multiprocessor (SM) executes thread blocks using its arithmetic and storage resources. A matrix-multiplication kernel may use Tensor Cores, while other kernels perform normalization, data rearrangement, or sampling. “Kernel,” “CUDA core,” “Tensor Core,” and “SM” name different things. NVIDIA CUDA Programming Guide, Programming Model (accessed October 9, 2026).

Compiler / graph optimizer
Transforms a model or program into an executable plan for the target hardware. It may fuse operations, choose layouts and numerical representations, and select specialized implementations.
Kernels / libraries
Implement individual operations or fused groups efficiently. Faster arithmetic units help only when the selected implementation uses them well.
Runtime
Loads executable artifacts, manages execution contexts and buffers, launches work, and coordinates dependencies. These duties overlap with compiler and framework responsibilities in real products.
Serving system
Accepts requests, routes them, manages batching and cache, enforces limits, streams output, and exposes service metrics. Fleet orchestration adds placement, scaling, health checks, updates, and recovery.

TensorRT provides a concrete example of the build/runtime distinction: a builder creates a GPU-specific engine and chooses implementations; a runtime loads and executes that engine. Supporting an operation is only the first hurdle. Dynamic shapes, numerical compatibility, version changes, and optimized implementation choices determine whether customer models run efficiently and reproducibly. NVIDIA TensorRT, How TensorRT Works (living documentation; accessed October 9, 2026).

Established mechanism: Continuous batching can replace completed sequences with new work without waiting for an entire fixed batch to finish. Orca developed iteration-level scheduling for this style of generative serving. Yu et al., Orca (OSDI, July 2022).

Analysis: scheduling is resource allocation. Chunking a long prefill can stop it monopolizing a step that also serves interactive decodes. Cache-aware routing can avoid repeated prefix computation, but concentrating cache hits on one worker can create a queue. The objective is not maximum batch size; it is useful throughput within latency and memory constraints. Dynamo documents routing decisions based on cached-prefix overlap and worker load. NVIDIA Dynamo, Router Design (accessed October 9, 2026).

Reliability is an end-to-end requirement. A correct arithmetic unit can still be undermined by bad memory, damaged links, inconsistent drivers, unstable power, or insufficient cooling. Error-correcting memory can correct certain faults and report others; it is not universal protection against silent numerical errors or software defects. NVIDIA’s diagnostic suite separately exercises memory, compute, PCIe/NVLink, power, thermal behavior, and collective communication. Diagnostics help identify or isolate a suspect resource; they do not repair it. NVIDIA DCGM, Diagnostics (accessed October 9, 2026).

Analysis: a credible recovery path detects a problem, removes the affected worker from new traffic, handles or retries interrupted requests according to policy, diagnoses the failure, repairs or replaces the component, and validates it before returning it to service. A lost decode worker may also lose KV state. Retrying can require recomputation and must not silently duplicate an agent’s external action. Monitoring should connect hardware signals—temperature, clocks, link errors, memory faults—to customer signals such as failed requests, queue delay, latency tails, and output quality.

Mechanism → customer outcome: Strong software converts silicon capability into available, predictable service; recovery and safe updates protect the value of that service over time.

Say it in an interview: “I would evaluate the accelerator, serving stack, and operational process as one product. I want a known-good workload, a repeatable deployment, visibility into bottlenecks, and a demonstrated failure-recovery path.” Follow-up: “What happens to live requests during a worker failure or model upgrade, and how is correctness checked after recovery?”

Added interview masterclass · Research cutoff: October 9, 2026

From a fast chip to a dependable inference business

The product is the useful work a customer can reliably obtain—not the largest number on a chip specification sheet. This addendum develops the system, manufacturing, and commercial implications of your pasted section. It supplements, and does not change, the original research.

How to read the evidence: “Company claim” identifies a statement by Etched, including its press releases. “Established principle” describes general engineering. “Analysis” is a reasoned implication, not a disclosure of Etched’s implementation. “Unknown” means the reviewed public material does not establish the answer.

1. Start with the exact state of the company

Company claim · June 30, 2026: Etched described a rack-scale inference product, reported A0 silicon from TSMC N4P, and said it was validating systems with customers. Its proposed differentiators were Low Voltage Inference (LVI) and Cluster Scale Memory (CSM). Etched’s technical announcement.

Company claim · July 23, 2026: Etched’s press release described its hardware as architecture-agnostic and said it was running DeepSeek, Qwen, and the non-transformer Mamba architecture. That is broader than a transformer-only description; it is not a published operator-by-operator compatibility guarantee. Company release distributed by GlobeNewswire.

Shipment and attributed customer testimony · August 18, 2026: Etched announced its first rack shipment to Jane Street and published a customer statement saying the rack was running in Jane Street’s data center. The announcement also reported a $700 million financing. This is meaningful deployment evidence, but it does not disclose throughput, uptime, production traffic volume, or customer-wide rollout. Jane Street is both customer and investor. Etched’s first-rack announcement. The same-day Etched press release dates the shipment to July 2026; the publication date is not the shipment date.

Reconcile older descriptions: June 2024 reporting described Sohu as transformer-specific; current company materials make a broader compatibility claim. TechCrunch · June 25, 2024. Do not describe either generation as a chip permanently containing one particular model’s weights. Model-family specialization and model-specific weights are different things.

Evidence ladder: A simulation predicts behavior; working silicon establishes that fabricated hardware functions; a rack test exercises integration; a shipment establishes delivery; sustained production establishes repeatable operation. One rung does not automatically establish the next. Funding supports execution capacity, not benchmark validity. Contracts are not recognized revenue. The public material reviewed here does not supply a reproducible independent rack benchmark or a fleet reliability history.

2. Low Voltage Inference: the opportunity and the hard part

Company claim: Etched says its math blocks operate below half the voltage of typical AI chips and that trillion-parameter sparse MoEs sustain over 80% of peak FLOPs without thermal throttling. It names co-design of arrays, scheduling, power delivery, packaging, and cooling. Etched · June 30, 2026.

Established principle: Pdynamic ≈ α × C × V² × f
α = switching activity; C = effective capacitance; V = supply voltage; f = switching frequency.

Switching transistor states charges and discharges electrical capacitance. Voltage appears squared, making it a powerful efficiency lever. As a strictly illustrative calculation, halving voltage while holding the other terms fixed gives one-quarter of that dynamic-power component. Those fixed conditions are not a prediction of real chip behavior. Intel power relationship · 2006 white paper.

Why it is difficult: Lower voltage generally reduces the timing margin available to circuits. A design must complete its calculations correctly despite manufacturing variation, changing temperature, and brief supply-voltage dips. Reducing frequency can help, but also reduces work per arithmetic unit per second. More parallel units can compensate only if data supply, scheduling, and workload parallelism keep them productive. Dreslinski et al. · February 2010 explains these low-voltage trade-offs; it does not establish Etched’s operating regime. This is the engineering question—not simply why everyone does not turn the voltage down.

Power delivery and cooling are different constraints. Voltage regulators convert the incoming supply to the rails circuits need; current changes can cause local voltage droop. Cooling removes heat after it is produced. Excellent cooling does not repair an inadequate power-delivery network, and a stable voltage rail does not remove a thermal hot spot. For equal power, lower voltage implies greater current through the relationship P = V × I; actual current depends on how much power the design saves.

Do not confuse dynamic power with total power. Leakage, memory, interconnects, host CPUs, voltage-conversion losses, fans or pumps, and facility cooling still matter. More compute density can increase total rack power even while improving energy per operation. Also distinguish thermal throttling from an electrical power cap, inadequate scheduling, or memory stalls: all can lower observed throughput, but they need different fixes.

Interview answer: “The plausible advantage is more sustained useful arithmetic within a power envelope. I would validate it with the customer’s model and precision, sustained clocks and power, output quality, and latency-constrained throughput—not convert a voltage ratio directly into a system-efficiency claim.” Deeper follow-up: What exactly counts as “peak” for a sparse model, which operations are counted, and over what duration?

3. Cluster Scale Memory: capacity is not locality

Company claim · July 23, 2026: Etched describes CSM as an SRAM/HBM hybrid memory subsystem with a shared SRAM pool across its scale-up domain, connected by a proprietary low-latency, high-bandwidth interconnect. This does not establish that all SRAM and HBM are one homogeneous, equally accessible memory pool. The disclosure does not specify the topology, coherence semantics, bandwidth under contention, or exact allocation policy. Etched’s July technical description.

Established principle: Pooling means software can use resources together; it does not make every byte equally close. An access can involve a local memory controller, a link, another device, arbitration, and a return trip. Latency is the time until a transfer completes; bandwidth is the amount transferable per second. Small dependent requests can be latency-sensitive even when total bandwidth is ample. Large streaming transfers can exhaust bandwidth despite individually short access times. NVIDIA’s NUMA documentation · accessed October 9, 2026 provides a concrete locality example, not a description of CSM.

Technical interpretation, not a disclosed implementation: A pooled design could improve model placement, reduce stranded capacity, and avoid unnecessary copies. But placing frequently reused state near its compute may still be essential. If many devices simultaneously target the same location, the destination or shared links can bottleneck. The useful question is therefore “how much accessible memory, at what effective bandwidth and latency, for this access pattern?”—not just “how large is the pool?”

Three memory ideas that should not be conflated: Capacity is how much state fits. Addressability is whether a device can refer to that state. Coherence determines how participants see updates to shared data. A system may offer pooling without ordinary CPU-style cache coherence or equal-cost access. Do not infer those properties from marketing language.

What to test: Measure local and remote access separately, then mixed traffic under realistic concurrency. Include long-context attention, MoE routing, memory-pressure behavior, and performance when multiple workloads share the domain. Record queueing and tail latency, not only average transfer time. Check whether a failed component forces a whole shared-memory domain to restart. These are proposed validation questions, not reported deficiencies in Etched hardware.

Interview answer: “CSM’s commercial promise is usable capacity with responsive access across a system. The important qualification is physical locality: shared memory still has a transport cost. I would ask how placement and contention affect goodput on the actual model.” Deeper follow-up: Which improvement comes from the interconnect, which from memory placement, and which from the serving scheduler?

4. Compatibility is a ladder, not a checkbox

Ask four separate questions: Can the model be represented? Can every required operation execute correctly? Can it achieve acceptable performance? Can the customer operate it reliably? A successful model demo answers much less than a supported production configuration.

Model weights and some execution choices can change in software. Physical datapaths, memory interfaces, and supported hardware operations have constraints. A new operator might compile into existing primitives, need a new optimized kernel, execute on a slower fallback path, or require a future hardware generation. Those possibilities have radically different commercial implications. Public architecture-agnostic language does not identify which applies.

For a customer, request a compatibility matrix covering exact model versions, maximum tested context, batch and parallelism configurations, numerical formats, quantization methods, sampling features, adapters, and custom operators. Ask who writes missing kernels, how correctness is checked, and how quickly new models are qualified. Do not infer specific FP8, FP4, BF16, or arbitrary-operator support where public documentation does not establish it.

NVIDIA’s software advantage is concrete: CUDA provides runtime interfaces and a compilation system with defined compatibility rules. An application can depend on framework integrations, libraries, custom kernels, communication software, profilers, and operational tooling—not merely a familiar API. CUDA binaries target particular GPU architectures; another vendor needs an appropriate implementation path, not a new logo on the same binary. NVIDIA CUDA platform documentation · accessed October 9, 2026.

Commercial implication: A migration can preserve the user-facing model API while requiring significant work underneath. Quantify integration effort, model-conversion time, missing features, performance tuning, and rollback. The strongest initial deployment may be a well-defined workload routed alongside an incumbent fleet rather than an immediate wholesale replacement.

Supplementary competitive update · September 28, 2026: Cerebras and Gimlet Labs named Gimlet a launch partner for CS-4 and reported that an integrated solution was already serving tokens in private deployments. The release does not establish that those existing deployments use CS-4. The proposed public datacenter later in 2026 and target of up to 3,000 tokens per second remain forward-looking, not a completed public deployment or independently reproduced benchmark. This illustrates why a buying comparison must distinguish present access from a future system promise. Joint company announcement · September 28, 2026.

5. The physical path from silicon to fleet

Established engineering, applied as analysis: These are the failure boundaries any accelerator supplier must manage. They are not claims that Etched has experienced these problems or uses a specific unpublished supplier configuration.

  1. Design and foundry. “Tape-out” hands the manufacturing design to the fabrication flow; it is not a working chip. First-silicon bring-up checks power, clocks, memory, links, and functional behavior. Yield is the fraction passing a defined test specification. A design that functions on a few parts may still be difficult to produce economically across manufacturing variation.
  2. Packaging and memory. Compute dies, memory stacks, substrates, and interconnects must become a functioning package. Advanced packaging connects these components at much greater density than an ordinary board. TSMC describes CoWoS as one such integration family; this explains the industry mechanism, not Etched’s undisclosed package selection. TSMC CoWoS overview · accessed October 9, 2026. Wafer, memory, substrate, and assembly capacity are separate dependencies; spare capacity in one does not compensate for a missing component in another.
  3. Boards and signal integrity. A printed circuit board must deliver clean power and carry high-speed signals within electrical margins. Poor connections, reflections, interference, or timing margins can cause errors and retries. A link that negotiates successfully is not necessarily reliable under prolonged traffic. Board inspection, electrical tests, traceability, and configuration control make failures diagnosable.
  4. Rack power and thermals. Power supplies, distribution, cabling, cold plates, manifolds, pumps, and facility heat rejection must work together. A cold plate transfers heat into coolant; a cooling distribution unit connects the equipment cooling loop to a facility heat-removal system. Liquid cooling does not mean every component is liquid-cooled or that facility requirements disappear. NVIDIA’s GB200 reference architecture, for example, describes hybrid liquid and air cooling. NVIDIA GB200 reference architecture · accessed October 9, 2026.
  5. Factory acceptance and installation. Test correctness, sustained load, thermal margins, links, firmware, and failure recovery before shipment; repeat relevant acceptance tests after installation. Site readiness includes electrical service, coolant conditions, weight and space limits, networking, and maintenance access. These decisions interact: a power-limited layout can spread equipment farther apart and change cable requirements. NVIDIA deployment-planning guide · accessed October 9, 2026.
  6. Fleet operation and repair. Track faults against hardware serial numbers, firmware, software, and workloads. Drain a failing worker, route requests elsewhere, preserve diagnostic evidence, replace the appropriate part, and requalify it. A useful support promise specifies detection, response, spares, replacement, and recovery—not only a warranty period. NVIDIA’s DCGM illustrates the expected category of telemetry: memory, links, power, thermal behavior, and device health. DCGM health monitoring · accessed October 9, 2026.

Why fleet scale changes the problem: A rare component failure becomes routine somewhere in a large deployment. Reliability includes fault containment: can one failure remain local, or does it interrupt a model spanning many devices? Availability also depends on repair time, spare capacity, routing, and model reloads. Rolling updates need canaries and rollback because a new compiler or kernel can change accuracy, latency, and stability together.

Interview answer: “Manufacturing and operations convert an architectural advantage into a repeatable service. I would want the sales commitment, site checklist, acceptance criteria, spares plan, and escalation owner to agree before promising a deployment date.” Deeper follow-up: What is the replaceable unit, and how much customer capacity is lost while it is repaired?

6. Design a pilot that could change a purchasing decision

Analysis: Define the decision before the benchmark. A latency-sensitive assistant, asynchronous document processor, and RL rollout farm have different acceptable delays, burst patterns, and failure costs. Favor an initial workload with supported models, substantial sustained demand, measurable economic pain, and a safe fallback. Sparse demand can make an otherwise efficient dedicated system uneconomical.

Proposed pilot scorecard—not Etched results
TestHold constant or recordDecision it informs
CorrectnessModel version, precision, quantization, tokenizer, sampling, task evaluations.Is the output equally useful? Identical sampled text is not required, but agreed quality is.
TrafficArrival timestamps, prompt/output distributions, cache reuse, bursts, cancellations.Does performance survive the customer’s real traffic instead of a favorable average?
Latency and loadTTFT, inter-token latency, end-to-end latency, throughput, percentile tails and error rate across a load sweep.What demand can be served while meeting the service-level objective?
System boundaryComplete server/rack count, software versions, host/network power, cooling boundary, warm-up.Is this an equivalent deployment comparison?
OperationsExtended runs, approved failure drills, model loading, upgrades, rollback and repair procedures.Can the customer sustain and recover the service?
EconomicsPrice or lease, installation, energy, support, integration labor, capacity headroom and utilization.Does the advantage survive total deployment cost and realistic demand?

Goodput: Define it explicitly for the pilot as output tokens belonging to successful requests that meet the agreed quality and latency requirements, divided by wall-clock time. For streaming, specify whether each gap or a per-request aggregate must pass. A high average token rate can coexist with unacceptable tail latency. NVIDIA’s serving guidance likewise evaluates TTFT, token latency, throughput, cache utilization, and failures rather than treating peak throughput as sufficient. NVIDIA Dynamo tuning guidance · accessed October 9, 2026.

Illustrative accounting definition—not a vendor result:
Cost per million qualifying output tokens = 1,000,000 × total cost during the period ÷ qualifying output tokens during the same period.

Include an allocated capital charge or lease, electricity, facility allocation, support, and agreed integration costs in the numerator. For this definition, input processing costs are included but input tokens are not in the denominator: therefore fix or disclose the input/output mix. Count retries’ resource consumption in cost, not duplicate output as useful work. For an hourly cost C and sustained qualifying output rate G tokens/second, the equivalent expression is 1,000,000C ÷ (3,600G). If G already incorporates idle periods and failures, do not apply another utilization discount.

Worked buying decision: faster capacity is not automatically a better purchase

Entirely hypothetical—not Etched, NVIDIA, or customer results. Compare two complete serving deployments, A and B, for the same model checkpoint, tokenizer, precision, sampling settings, and agreed task-quality threshold. For simple arithmetic, every request has 1,024 input tokens and 256 output tokens; an actual pilot must replay the customer’s length and arrival distributions. Both pass the same assumed gate: at least 99% of submitted requests complete successfully with TTFT no greater than 1 second and average TPOT no greater than 50 milliseconds. Count output only from passing requests; include failed work and input processing in cost.

Assume the pilot establishes capacity for 10,000 qualifying output tokens/second on A and 15,000 on B at those gates. The customer needs the same 5,000 qualifying output tokens/second averaged across a 30-day month on either deployment, including idle periods. Assume the traffic replay confirms both can absorb its bursts and deliver that demand. Their purchased capacities are therefore used at 50% and about 33.3%, respectively; these are demand-to-qualified-capacity ratios, not GPU arithmetic utilization. Both deliver 5,000 × 3,600 × 720 = 12.96 billion qualifying output tokens per month.

Assumed costs in US dollars; identical monthly useful output
Monthly accounting itemDeployment ADeployment B
Recurring deployment cost$24,000$16,000
One-time incremental migration cost$0$48,000
Migration allocation over 12 months$0/month$4,000/month
Total monthly cost on that horizon$24,000$20,000
Cost per million qualifying output tokens$24,000 ÷ 12,960 ≈ $1.85$20,000 ÷ 12,960 ≈ $1.54

The recurring estimates are assumed to include a lease, energy at the agreed facility boundary, networking, support, operations labor, and reserved recovery capacity at this demand. B’s one-time amount covers integration, validation, and transition work; do not charge it again elsewhere. The comparison assumes flat recurring costs, no residual migration value, and no financing, tax, or discount-rate differences. Over 12 months B is about 16.7% cheaper per useful output token despite its lower capacity-use ratio. Its headline capacity advantage alone did not decide the purchase.

Stress test that reverses the choice: Suppose the supported workload will last only four months before a model change makes a new qualification necessary, and this comparison assigns no benefit to B’s migration work beyond those four months. B’s allocation becomes $48,000 ÷ 4 = $12,000/month. Its total is now $28,000/month, or about $2.16 per million qualifying output tokens; A remains about $1.85. Across four months A costs $96,000 and B costs $112,000 for the same useful output. The undiscounted break-even horizon is $48,000 ÷ ($24,000 − $16,000) = 6 months. This is an assumption test, not a prediction of either platform’s lifespan.

Decision and interview takeaway: “On these assumptions I would choose B for a validated 12-month workload, but A for four months. Before deciding, I would test how durable compatibility is, whether the quality and latency gates survive real bursts and failures, and whether migration estimates include all teams’ work. I would not multiply monthly output by utilization again—it already includes idle time.”

Power accounting: Tokens per joule equals useful tokens divided by measured energy over the same interval. Chip power, server input power, rack power, and facility power are different boundaries. PUE is facility energy divided by IT energy; applying it to an IT measurement is an approximation for allocating facility overhead, not a way to infer unmeasured chip efficiency. Always state the boundary and interval. U.S. Department of Energy design guide · July 2024.

The purchasing question: “At our quality and latency targets, how much dependable work can we deliver per dollar and per constrained megawatt, including the cost of adopting and operating the system?”

7. Connect reasoning, agents, and post-training without conflating them

Longer reasoning outputs increase sequential decode work. Parallel candidate answers increase concurrent work and memory demand. Agent loops add repeated prompts, tool waits, growing histories, and variable response lengths. Prefix reuse can save repeated prompt computation, but it requires cache capacity and appropriate routing. External tools can dominate end-to-end latency even when model execution accelerates. NVIDIA Dynamo explicitly treats routing, cache management, and movement between workers as serving-system responsibilities. Dynamo architecture · version 0.7.0, accessed October 9, 2026.

Rollouts are inference inside a training workflow. The current policy generates candidate actions or answers; an environment or evaluator returns outcomes; a training process computes updates; refreshed weights reach rollout workers. Backpropagation and optimizer updates are not ordinary inference. Faster generation can help only the portion it accelerates, and moving updated weights, evaluating rewards, or waiting for long trajectories can become the new limit. The APRIL paper studies long-tail rollout lengths in a specific RL setting; its runtime proportions should not be generalized to every training run. APRIL · September 23, 2025.

Analysis for Etched: Rollout acceleration is a plausible application to investigate, not an established product capability here. The reviewed Etched announcements do not provide an end-to-end RL benchmark or validated weight-synchronization workflow. Ask about rapid weight refresh, log-probability outputs, numerical consistency with the training engine, rollout-length variance, and integration with the customer’s RL framework.

Your AI supply-chain connection: The accelerator supplies computation; an RL environment supplies tasks, transitions, feedback, and verifiable outcomes. Better hardware can produce more attempts, but weak rewards or unrepresentative environments can still produce poor learning. Evaluate cost per useful trajectory or successful task alongside tokens per second. More generated tokens are not automatically more intelligence.

8. A precise interview explanation

“I think the core challenge is turning a silicon advantage into dependable customer capacity. A customer buys an inference outcome: the right model and quality, acceptable response times, predictable cost, and reliable operation. Compute, memory, interconnects, scheduling, power, and cooling jointly determine that outcome. Optimizing only one layer can just move the bottleneck.

“The architecture questions I would pursue are whether lower-voltage compute improves sustained useful work within the customer’s power budget, and whether the memory system delivers accessible capacity without losing its latency benefit under contention. I would separate what the company has demonstrated from what still needs workload-specific validation.

“Commercially, I would start with a narrow deployment where demand is substantial, compatibility is clear, and the buyer has a measurable problem. The pilot should use their models, quality evaluations, and traffic distribution. It should measure goodput under latency targets, energy at an agreed system boundary, and the integration and operational work required.

“Then I would test repeatability: site readiness, supply commitments, acceptance tests, software upgrades, monitoring, recovery, and support. Those are product features because they affect uptime, utilization, and customer trust. A cheaper token in a controlled benchmark is not necessarily a cheaper dependable service.

“My interest in post-training adds another question: can this system economically generate useful rollouts while another system performs learning updates? I would not assume that inference acceleration accelerates gradients, or that tokens alone measure learning value. I would want to understand weight refresh, evaluator bottlenecks, and the quality of the environment.

“For a commercially oriented role, the contribution is translating those engineering constraints into an honest qualification process and bringing customer requirements back into product decisions. I would want to help the team sell a validated operating advantage, with a clear understanding of where it applies and what remains unproven.”
Questions that open a serious conversation
  1. Which workload has the clearest measured advantage today, and which does not? Establishes product focus and honesty about fit.
  2. Which latency and quality constraints define the benchmark you trust most? Converts an ambiguous speed claim into a customer outcome.
  3. What is the process and typical engineering work to qualify a newly released model? Tests practical programmability rather than a slogan.
  4. What changes for a customer between a successful pilot and its second production deployment? Surfaces repeatability, support, and supply-chain requirements.
  5. Which site constraints disqualify a prospect before a pilot? Protects both the customer and sales engineering from a technically impressive but undeployable win.
  6. What would need to be true to make rollout generation a supported workload? Connects your research interests while acknowledging the missing evidence.
