10

Reasoning agents and reinforcement learning

Reasoning can increase generated-token counts before a final answer. Agent workflows add successive model calls, tool responses, and growing histories. Long context raises prefill work and retained state; multi-turn reuse can also make prefix caching valuable. Faster token generation helps only while generation is on the application’s critical path. Slow tools, external APIs, retries, and human approvals can dominate total task time. MLCommons’ agentic benchmarking work explicitly treats multi-turn cache locality and per-user progress as system concerns. Agentic inference methodology

RL iteration
Policy weights → generate actions and trajectories
    ↔ tools or environment steps
    → verifier or reward → training loss
    → backpropagation and optimizer → updated weights
    → synchronize rollout workers → repeat

Principle. Rollout generation executes a policy to collect outputs or action trajectories. That generation is inference. Learning then computes losses and gradients and updates the model. Environments, rewards, tool execution, and policy synchronization introduce additional costs. The verl framework illustrates separate rollout and training workers and explicit weight synchronization. verl workers

Dedicated inference hardware could serve rollout workers while other resources perform training. This is an architectural possibility, not a demonstrated Etched integration. It requires suitable sampling, log probabilities where the algorithm needs them, tokenizer/model consistency, timely synchronization of updated policy weights, and an acceptable level of policy-version lag. Asynchronous rollouts can improve overlap but complicate freshness and scheduling. verl asynchronous training

Our toy calculation. If generation consumes 80 units of a 100-unit iteration and becomes twice as fast, total time becomes 80 ÷ 2 + 20 = 60 units. The overall speedup is 100 ÷ 60 = 1.67×. If environment execution dominates instead, the benefit shrinks. This is why faster tokens and faster learning are different measurements.

What Etched publicly says about RL

Etched’s July update explicitly recruits for RL environments for recursive kernel generation. Its Agent Research role adds engineering environments, evaluation of correctness/reliability/efficiency, and SFT, RL, and distillation with the harness in the loop. This supports an internal software-improvement and engineering-agent strategy. It does not establish commercial rollout-product availability, backpropagation support on Etched silicon, or where the company’s own optimizer runs. Etched July update Agent Research role

Your research connection — analysis. An engineering environment could let a model propose a kernel, compile it, test correctness, and measure runtime. Reward design then matters: a faster incorrect kernel is not an improvement, and timing artifacts can be exploited. Tests need varied shapes and inputs, honest timing, and evaluation on held-out cases. This connects your environment-supply-chain work directly to the reliability of hardware/software optimization.

A useful question is: “In your kernel-generation environments, how do you balance correctness, speed, and generalization to unseen shapes—and how does an improvement move into the production runtime?” That asks about a publicly described effort without pretending to know its proprietary implementation.

11

Explanations to rehearse aloud

These scripts synthesize the evidence and reasoning above. Adapt the language to your own voice. Timing assumes conversational delivery; pause to define a term when your listener needs it.

Thirty seconds

Etched is building complete systems for running AI models. Its thesis is that inference improves when compute, memory, networking, power, and software are designed together. The customer promise is more useful output at an acceptable response time and cost. What interests me is the transition from early hardware validation to repeatable deployments, where technical performance, software integration, and operational execution all have to work.

Two minutes

I understand Etched as an inference-systems company. Running a model involves much more than having enough arithmetic units. The system must move weights and intermediate state, communicate across chips, schedule requests, and stay within power and cooling limits.

A request usually has two different phases. Prefill processes the prompt and often provides enough parallel work to use matrix hardware efficiently. Decode generates the continuation, where a single stream may spend much of its time moving weights and reading cached attention state. More batching can improve reuse, but it can also change the response time each user sees.

Etched’s public design centers on lower-voltage computation and a memory system organized across its cluster. The intended benefits are sustained arithmetic within a power envelope and faster access to the data needed for generation. The important diligence question is how those benefits hold across actual models, context lengths, and traffic patterns.

I would evaluate the product through useful throughput at a required quality and latency, then include migration, utilization, reliability, and support in the cost. I would also ask how quickly new models become supported and optimized. A compelling hardware measurement is the beginning of a customer decision; dependable operation determines whether that decision scales.

My interest in post-training environments also connects to Etched’s discussion of kernel-generation environments. Measuring correctness and speed well is essential if model-generated software is going to improve the system.

Five minutes

Etched’s opportunity comes from a basic feature of AI inference: the customer experiences a complete system. Response time and cost depend on arithmetic, data movement, scheduling, communication, power, and operational reliability. Improving one component helps only when that component is limiting useful work.

Consider a model reading a long document. First, the text becomes tokens and the system processes those tokens through the model’s layers. That prefill phase constructs attention state and produces the scores used to choose the first output token. The model then continues generating, repeatedly using its weights and the stored keys and values for earlier positions. This retained state is the KV cache. It grows with context and with the number of concurrent sequences.

Prefill often has many known token positions to process together, which allows substantial reuse of weights. A single decode stream provides less reuse per step. That is why memory movement can dominate even when a chip has enormous peak arithmetic capacity. In a toy dense model example, reading 140 GB of weights at 3 TB/s takes about 47 milliseconds. If the arithmetic itself takes only one millisecond, doubling arithmetic capacity barely changes that limiting read time. Real systems are more complicated, but the example explains why peak FLOPs alone is inadequate.

Batching changes the situation. Several requests can reuse the same weights during a step, improving throughput. But batching can increase waiting or execution time, and each request brings its own attention state. Sparse expert models add another dimension: they activate only part of their weights for each token, but tokens must reach the selected experts. Communication and uneven demand can leave capacity idle. So a long prompt, a single interactive user, and a high-concurrency service can have different bottlenecks on the same hardware.

Etched’s two public design themes address sustained computation and memory access. Lower voltage can reduce switching power, although the familiar voltage-squared relationship applies to one power component and does not directly predict rack savings. Its cluster memory approach combines SRAM and HBM with an interconnect. That raises useful questions about capacity, placement, remote-access latency, and contention. The design is promising if those choices improve delivered performance under realistic constraints; the marketing description alone cannot settle that.

I would also distinguish running a model from supporting it well. The system needs correct numerics, efficient kernels, a runtime, serving integration, and a path to future operators. Software can materially improve existing hardware, and competitors are doing that continuously. A fair evaluation therefore needs a current comparison with matching model quality, prompt and output distributions, latency targets, and full-system boundaries.

Commercially, I would start with a representative workload and define success before the pilot. Measure usable throughput, tail latency, power, failures, and operational effort. Include installation, migration, spares, idle capacity, and support in the economics. Then establish delivery and model-support commitments before expansion. A customer can begin with a suitable workload segment rather than make an all-or-nothing infrastructure change.

My connection to the company is through how capabilities become reliable products. In post-training research, a useful environment must measure the behavior that matters and resist misleading shortcuts. The same applies to kernel-generation environments: correctness tests and trustworthy performance measurements determine whether an apparent improvement is real. I would be interested in how those experiments connect to the production runtime and customer experience.

12

Fifteen questions to practice

The answers below are analytical coaching, not statements about your employment history. For behavioral questions, substitute a real example and verifiable outcome from your own work.

1 Why are you interested in Etched

I’m interested in the point where a technical advantage has to become a dependable customer system. My research into AI infrastructure and post-training has made me attentive to the whole chain: the capability being improved, the measurement, and the operational work required to deliver it. Etched gives those questions concrete consequences in latency, power, production, and adoption.

Deeper follow-up: What would you contribute personally? Connect a real project to customer discovery, execution, or a repeatable operating process. Specify your own decisions and results; do not invent metrics.

2 How would you explain the product to a buyer

Start with the buyer’s workload and service target. Etched supplies a system intended to execute models efficiently across compute, memory, networking, and software. I would translate the design into the buyer’s outcome: faster responses, more useful work within a power allocation, or lower delivered cost. Then I would identify what must be measured to substantiate that outcome.

Deeper follow-up: What would you ask before discussing speed? Ask for the model, quality bar, prompt/output distribution, concurrency, latency targets, and existing deployment constraints.

3 Why can a fast chip produce a slow service

The chip can wait for weights, cached attention state, another device, or scheduled work. Requests can also wait in queues or on external tools. Thermal limits may reduce sustained clocks. I would profile where time goes and distinguish device execution from end-to-end request latency before recommending more hardware.

Deeper follow-up: What evidence would you request? A latency breakdown, memory and communication counters, utilization traces, queue depth, and behavior across offered load.

4 Explain prefill and decode

Prefill processes known prompt positions and constructs attention state. Decode extends the sequence using previous state. Prefill often has enough parallel work to stress arithmetic; small-batch decode often stresses memory movement. The balance changes with batching, context, model structure, and software. I would avoid assigning every request a permanent compute-bound or memory-bound label.

Deeper follow-up: Could decode become compute-bound? Yes. More weight reuse across a large batch can make arithmetic limiting; attention and communication can create other limits.

5 What is the KV cache and why does it matter

It holds keys and values for earlier tokens so attention can reuse them. Each active sequence needs retained state, so context length and concurrency consume memory together. Cache allocation can determine how many requests fit, while cache reads can limit generation. The architecture and number of KV heads affect the size.

Deeper follow-up: Does PagedAttention shrink every token’s mathematical state? No. It improves allocation and sharing; compression or architectural changes address different parts of the problem.

6 What makes mixture of experts difficult to serve

Only selected experts execute for a token, reducing active work relative to total stored capacity. The system still has to place the experts, route tokens, and handle imbalance. A popular expert can become a bottleneck while others sit idle. I would inspect the distribution of work and communication, not use activated parameter count as a complete cost estimate.

Deeper follow-up: Why add expert parallelism? It distributes expert storage and work, but creates token dispatch and return traffic that must be efficiently scheduled.

7 Why should lower voltage help

The dynamic switching component of power scales approximately with voltage squared at fixed activity, capacitance, and frequency. That creates a strong incentive to lower voltage. The challenge is maintaining correct timing and useful throughput. Total system savings also depend on memory, links, leakage, and power delivery, so I would not translate a voltage ratio directly into a rack-efficiency claim.

Deeper follow-up: What would validate the benefit? Correct outputs and sustained useful throughput at measured system power across representative operating conditions.

8 What would you ask about shared cluster memory

I would ask how data is placed, which accesses are local or remote, and how latency and bandwidth change under concurrency. A shared pool can improve resource use, but it still has a physical topology. I would also ask how failures are isolated and which workloads benefit enough to offset any new coordination costs.

Deeper follow-up: Does sharing imply uniform latency or coherence? No. Those are separate implementation properties that require explicit documentation.

9 How would you validate a performance claim

I would reproduce it with a fixed model and quality threshold, then vary load, prompt length, output length, and context. I would record full hardware and software configuration and compare useful throughput within the same latency targets. Power and cost must cover the same system boundary. I would examine the curve rather than choose a single favorable point.

Deeper follow-up: What if quantization differs? Permit it if the customer’s quality target is satisfied, disclose the difference, and avoid presenting it as a pure hardware comparison.

10 Why choose Etched over an established alternative

A buyer would need a sufficiently large and durable benefit for a suitable workload. That benefit could be capacity under a power constraint, interactive speed, or delivered cost. It must exceed migration, support, and supplier risk. I would identify a concrete workload segment and validate it; I would not assume every customer should move every model.

Deeper follow-up: What is the strongest incumbent advantage? Existing software, operating familiarity, support and supply relationships, and the ability to reuse infrastructure across workloads.

11 How would you prioritize limited supply

I would combine workload fit, readiness to deploy, likelihood of a successful reference, learning value, expansion potential, economics, and support burden. A large contract that cannot be installed or integrated may create less value than a prepared customer with a repeatable use case. I would make the allocation criteria explicit across commercial, production, and engineering teams.

Deeper follow-up: What if a prestigious customer needs extensive customization? Quantify the engineering opportunity cost and the reusable learning before treating prestige as decisive.

12 How would you evaluate customer economics

Estimate the cost of meeting the workload’s quality and service targets over time. Include equipment or service charges, energy, facilities, networking, support, spares, migration, redundancy, and utilization. Divide by useful work actually delivered. For agents, I would also use successful task completion because tokens can include retries and unproductive reasoning.

Deeper follow-up: Which assumption would you stress-test first? Often utilization, but the right answer depends on whether the buyer is power-limited, latency-limited, or integration-limited.

13 How does inference hardware connect to RL

Generating policy trajectories is inference, so specialized hardware could accelerate that stage. The learning loop also includes environments, rewards, gradients, optimizer work, and weight synchronization. I would measure the complete iteration and ask about policy freshness and training-stack integration. Internal RL for software optimization is a separate use case from selling rollout acceleration.

Deeper follow-up: Why might faster rollouts fail to speed learning? Environments or training may dominate, weight refresh may be costly, or asynchronous data may become stale.

14 What could invalidate Etched technical advantage

A shift in model operators or access patterns could reduce utilization; competitors could improve the same bottleneck; or gains could narrow at realistic load and context. Production, integration, or reliability costs could erase a hardware advantage. I would watch model-enablement time and the performance/cost curve over successive software and hardware releases.

Deeper follow-up: Does broad architecture support eliminate that risk? No. Executing a model and executing it competitively are different claims.

15 How do you work with engineers on an uncertain commitment

Clarify the customer outcome and identify what is known, assumed, and untested. Translate the request into measurable acceptance criteria and a small experiment. Agree on who owns the result and communicate the limitation accurately. Once there is evidence, turn the successful workflow into a repeatable process. Use a real example to show how you have done this.

Deeper follow-up: What if the customer wants a promise before testing? Offer a scoped pilot and explicit conditions; describe which evidence is needed before committing to production performance.

13

Eight questions for the interviewer

Choose four or five based on the interviewer. Ask for publicly discussable examples and follow the answer rather than reciting the entire list.

1. “For which workload does your current system show the clearest customer advantage, and where is that advantage smallest?” This tests workload segmentation and technical judgment.

2. “When LVI and CSM work as intended, which constraint limits the next improvement?” This opens a discussion of the next system constraint without presupposing a particular result.

3. “What happens between a new model release and an optimized, supported deployment on Etched?” This reveals compatibility, numerical validation, compiler, and support work.

4. “What has changed in the product or deployment process because of the first customer rack?” This turns early validation into concrete operational learning.

5. “What does a customer need to prove during a pilot before you both feel ready to expand?” This clarifies acceptance criteria and ownership of adoption risk.

6. “Which production or support constraint most affects delivery predictability today?” This connects commercial planning to physical execution.

7. “How do your kernel-generation environments measure correctness, speed, and generalization, and how do improvements reach production?” This connects your post-training research to a public company initiative.

8. “For this role, what important decision or process should I own within the first three months, and which teams would depend on it?” This reveals practical scope and success criteria.

14

Misconceptions and a concise glossary

Avoid saying that more FLOPs always means more tokens; that decode is always memory-bound; that model weights are the entire memory footprint; or that fewer active MoE parameters mean the inactive experts need no storage. Shared memory does not automatically mean uniform access. Lower voltage does not imply proportional rack savings. Low-bit storage does not imply every operation uses that arithmetic format.

For Etched specifically, avoid presenting broad compatibility as a guarantee of arbitrary future models, a shipment as fleet-scale proof, contracts as recognized revenue, or investor enthusiasm as an independent benchmark. Do not carry old Sohu speedup ratios into current claims. Do not equate an internal RL research program with demonstrated hardware support for all stages of training.

Term

Meaning

ASIC

Integrated circuit designed for a particular class of applications

A0 silicon

First manufactured revision; working does not mean bug-free or fully qualified

FLOP and FLOP/s

A floating-point operation; operations per second

Arithmetic intensity

Operations performed per byte moved at a specified memory boundary

SRAM and HBM

Fast, area-intensive memory; stacked high-bandwidth DRAM with larger capacity

KV cache

Retained attention keys and values for previous tokens

GQA and MLA

Grouped-query attention; Multi-head Latent Attention, each changing attention-state costs

MoE

Mixture of experts, with token-dependent selection of expert networks

Collective

Tightly connected compute domain; adding domains or systems through a broader network

TTFT and TPOT

Time to first token; average time per subsequent output token

SLO

Service-level objective, a measurable operating target

TCO

Total cost of ownership over an explicit period and workload

New product introduction; surface-mount assembly of components onto boards

Rollout and policy lag

Generated action trajectory; difference between generating-policy and current-policy versions

Two hours through the expanded guide

This is a prioritized route, not an instruction to finish every page. Read the linked essentials, close the explanation, and answer aloud. The goal is a mechanism you can explain, a customer consequence, and an honest boundary on the evidence.

  1. 00–15 minutes · Establish the evidenceRead the brief, then the Etched claim ledger. Explain the current rack-scale proposition, what changed from the historical Sohu description, and why a shipment is not a fleet benchmark. Keep company assertions distinct from measured customer outcomes.
  2. 15–40 minutes · Trace one requestUse the request and attention walkthrough, then redo the three original examples. Explain why old K/V can be reused, what grows with context, and why more FLOPs may not help. Prioritize the arithmetic over memorizing every GPU specification.
  3. 40–60 minutes · Follow the bottleneckRead compute and batching, memory, and communication across chips. Trace the actual data moving, then use the GPU comparison guidance to distinguish MoE sparsity from sparse Tensor Core performance.
  4. 60–80 minutes · Apply the mechanism to EtchedStudy Low Voltage Inference, Cluster Scale Memory, and compatibility. For each: state the constraint, proposed mechanism, trade-off, customer outcome, and measurement needed. Do not fill undisclosed architecture details with guesses.
  5. 80–100 minutes · Make a customer decisionWork through the hypothetical pilot economics, then silicon-to-fleet delivery. Explain which assumption reverses the choice, which site requirement can block installation, and what must hold before expanding a pilot.
  6. 100–120 minutes · Rehearse and retrieveRead the RL loop, rehearse the two-minute explanation, and answer the five checks below without notes. Choose four interviewer questions. Prepare a real example of your own work; do not adopt the guide’s hypothetical examples as personal achievements.

Optional depth: Return to GPU families and format support, detailed power/cooling discussions, and primary-source reading after the core mechanisms feel natural. For GTM, prioritize qualification and economics; for operations, deployment and recovery; for technical strategy, workload changes and programmability.

Five explain-it-without-notes checks

Try an answer first. Open the checkpoint to assess the reasoning, not to memorize its wording.

1. Why cache old keys and values rather than old queries?

In conventional causal decoder attention, adding a later token does not change earlier tokens’ per-layer keys and values. The current query is matched against those retained keys to combine their values. Old queries are unnecessary for computing only the new position. Reading and attending to a longer retained history still requires work. Review the attention mechanism.

2. Why can batching improve total throughput without making each user faster?

Several positions can reuse a weight read, but the step also does more arithmetic and accesses more sequence state. Total output counts every request’s new token; a single user does not receive the whole batch’s output. Queueing and longer steps can increase latency, and long-context cache traffic can become limiting. Review the batch example.

3. Does a sparse MoE automatically qualify for sparse GPU FLOPs?

No. Conditional expert selection skips unselected networks. Structured sparse matrix hardware requires a supported pattern within its operands; MoE routing alone does not establish that pattern. Check precision, sparsity conditions, and what the quoted operation count means. Review the two meanings of sparse.

4. Why do lower voltage and pooled memory not prove better customer economics?

Lower voltage affects switching power but can affect timing and frequency; other power costs remain. Shared capacity still has locality, transport, contention, and failure boundaries. Require correct results, quality-qualified throughput under latency targets, measured system energy, reliability, and a complete cost comparison. Review LVI and CSM.

5. Why is twice-as-fast rollout generation only a 1.67× iteration speedup in the toy example?

The original example starts with 80 units of generation and 20 units of other work: 80 ÷ 2 + 20 = 60, so 100 ÷ 60 ≈ 1.67. The estimate assumes the remaining work and workload stay fixed. Environment delays, synchronization, policy lag, changed output lengths, or a new bottleneck can reduce the realized gain. Review the original assumptions.
